items.content: © IM Imagery - stock.adobe.com Summary · The share of firms using AI in EU strategic sectors grew from 7% in 2021 to 18% in 2025: media, energy and electronic sectors lead, while mobility, tourism and agri-food lag behind · The analysis and the methodology developed by the JRC allow to measure and monitor AI uptake and barriers to use in the strategic sectors, covered by the Apply AI strategy · The growth of AI use is mainly driven by LLMs as they have become more accessible and available at lower cost · Sector-specific measures for AI adoption are essential for a deeper integration of AI into core processes The share of firms using AI in EU strategic sectors grew from 7% in 2021 to 18% in 2025, according to a new JRC analysis. While each of the 10 sectors advanced in use of AI, the growth was uneven, driven mainly by accessible, general-purpose AI — systems that analyse or generate text, code, images, sound and video. The analysis and the methodology developed allow to measure and monitor the levels and development of AI usage, types of deployments and barriers to its adoption in the strategic sectors covered by the Apply AI Strategy . Launched a year ago, the strategy aims to boost AI uptake and encourages organisations to consider the opportunities and risks posed by AI solutions to improve processes, efficiency and competitiveness. It proposes specific actions to support the adoption of relevant AI use cases in strategic sectors. The 10 strategic sectors are essential for EU economic security, green and digital transitions, and defence readiness. They include agri-food, climate (climate and environment); defence (defence, security and space); electronic (electronic communications); energy, manufacturing (manufacturing, engineering and construction); media (cultural and creative sectors, and media); mobility (mobility, transport and automotive); pharma (healthcare, including pharmaceuticals) and tourism. Considering the whole EU economic areas besides the strategic ones, the share of firms adopting the use of AI is slightly higher: it grew from 8% in 2021 to 20% in 2025. The analysis drew on the Eurostat’s ICT enterprise survey data collected between 2021 and 2025, based on the EU classification of economic activities (NACE) . It assesses adoption levels, technologies, applications and adoption barriers across them. The results are published in the report AI adoption across European strategic sectors . What are the AI adoption trends in strategic sectors? Firms in the cultural and creative sectors, media, energy, and electronic communications are leading the AI adoption with respectively 38%, 34% and 30 % of firms using AI . In these sectors, AI is used for a variety of business functions, from ICT security to R&D and production, demonstrating a broader diffusion of the technology. In contrast, mobility, tourism and agri ‑ food are the sectors presenting the lowest uptake. In these, AI applications are still confined to marketing, sales, and other accessible tasks. Manufacturing and climate industries show a mixed pattern, combining ready-to-use AI tools with a modest shift towards using AI in production processes. In general, the increased AI adoption is mainly driven by AI systems analysing and generating written or audio output for marketing and sales purposes, technologies which have become more accessible and are available at a lower cost. From tools to core processes, different adoption patterns across strategic sectors While the overall adoption curve is positive, the analysis highlights that in many cases AI still needs to be embedded into core business processes , such as production, where the greatest productivity gains are possible. Firms that tailor AI and integrate it into their production, workflows or infrastructure tend to achieve higher value-added outcomes, leveraging data and expertise. The differences between capital-intensive industries, typically requiring sophisticated computing infrastructure, and labour-intensive sectors, based on people and skills, play also a role for understanding AI adoption. The data show that the capital-intensive sectors, such as energy and electronics, are experiencing a stronger growth in AI uptake than sectors more balanced in terms of capital and labour. Between 2021 and 2025, AI-uptake of energy firms grew from 18% to 34%, while electronics from 12% to 30%. A sector-specific approach is needed to support AI adoption The analysis highlights three key components when looking at how firms adopt AI: how much a company has reorganised its way of working to take full advantage of AI, how much it uses AI in production , and to what extent it is adopting ready-to-use AI solutions vs custom made ones, the level of AI commoditisation . Ranking of sectors in key components AI- enhanced organisation, production and AI commoditisation. Source: JRC, based on Eurostat’s survey on ICT usage in enterprises (isoc_e). The ranking of strategic sectors along these key components shows a positive correlation between organisation and production. The firms investing more in structural organisational changes to integrate AI are more likely to use AI in production, suggesting that organisational changes must be prioritised. This is the case of energy, electronic communications or defence industries. The analysis reveals that the use of ready-to-use AI solutions vs custom-made ones depends on the specificities of each sector. For instance, the climate sector, despite having a medium AI uptake, displays a low uptake of off-the-shelf AI solutions, as it requires a higher degree of customisation compared to other strategic sectors. At the same time, the manufacturing sector, overall displaying a low AI uptake, ranks higher than climate for adopting off-the-shelf solutions. This indicates that using accessible ready-to-use AI solutions does not necessarily increase integration of AI into production processes. Overall, the analysis suggests that policy measures aimed at increasing AI integration into core processes need to be tailored to the specificities of the strategic sector. Bottlenecks to AI adoption The data show that the lack of relevant expertise is widely indicated as the main obstacle to AI adoption across the vast majority of strategic sectors. In particular, two factors emerge as the dominant bottlenecks: the scarcity of specialised skills and the regulatory uncertainty, including concerns about data protection and privacy. The report suggests that digitalisation initiatives, skills development, and organisational change can support AI uptake and close the gap between tool uptake to deeper integration. The results of the study will support policy makers with setting targets and create new sector-specific measures on how to increase AI adoption in the strategic economic areas. items.raw_text: © IM Imagery - stock.adobe.com Summary · The share of firms using AI in EU strategic sectors grew from 7% in 2021 to 18% in 2025: media, energy and electronic sectors lead, while mobility, tourism and agri-food lag behind · The analysis and the methodology developed by the JRC allow to measure and monitor AI uptake and barriers to use in the strategic sectors, covered by the Apply AI strategy · The growth of AI use is mainly driven by LLMs as they have become more accessible and available at lower cost · Sector-specific measures for AI adoption are essential for a deeper integration of AI into core processes The share of firms using AI in EU strategic sectors grew from 7% in 2021 to 18% in 2025, according to a new JRC analysis. While each of the 10 sectors advanced in use of AI, the growth was uneven, driven mainly by accessible, general-purpose AI — systems that analyse or generate text, code, images, sound and video. The analysis and the methodology developed allow to measure and monitor the levels and development of AI usage, types of deployments and barriers to its adoption in the strategic sectors covered by the Apply AI Strategy . Launched a year ago, the strategy aims to boost AI uptake and encourages organisations to consider the opportunities and risks posed by AI solutions to improve processes, efficiency and competitiveness. It proposes specific actions to support the adoption of relevant AI use cases in strategic sectors. The 10 strategic sectors are essential for EU economic security, green and digital transitions, and defence readiness. They include agri-food, climate (climate and environment); defence (defence, security and space); electronic (electronic communications); energy, manufacturing (manufacturing, engineering and construction); media (cultural and creative sectors, and media); mobility (mobility, transport and automotive); pharma (healthcare, including pharmaceuticals) and tourism. Considering the whole EU economic areas besides the strategic ones, the share of firms adopting the use of AI is slightly higher: it grew from 8% in 2021 to 20% in 2025. The analysis drew on the Eurostat’s ICT enterprise survey data collected between 2021 and 2025, based on the EU classification of economic activities (NACE) . It assesses adoption levels, technologies, applications and adoption barriers across them. The results are published in the report AI adoption across European strategic sectors . What are the AI adoption trends in strategic sectors? Firms in the cultural and creative sectors, media, energy, and electronic communications are leading the AI adoption with respectively 38%, 34% and 30 % of firms using AI . In these sectors, AI is used for a variety of business functions, from ICT security to R&D and production, demonstrating a broader diffusion of the technology. In contrast, mobility, tourism and agri ‑ food are the sectors presenting the lowest uptake. In these, AI applications are still confined to marketing, sales, and other accessible tasks. Manufacturing and climate industries show a mixed pattern, combining ready-to-use AI tools with a modest shift towards using AI in production processes. In general, the increased AI adoption is mainly driven by AI systems analysing and generating written or audio output for marketing and sales purposes, technologies which have become more accessible and are available at a lower cost. From tools to core processes, different adoption patterns across strategic sectors While the overall adoption curve is positive, the analysis highlights that in many cases AI still needs to be embedded into core business processes , such as production, where the greatest productivity gains are possible. Firms that tailor AI and integrate it into their production, workflows or infrastructure tend to achieve higher value-added outcomes, leveraging data and expertise. The differences between capital-intensive industries, typically requiring sophisticated computing infrastructure, and labour-intensive sectors, based on people and skills, play also a role for understanding AI adoption. The data show that the capital-intensive sectors, such as energy and electronics, are experiencing a stronger growth in AI uptake than sectors more balanced in terms of capital and labour. Between 2021 and 2025, AI-uptake of energy firms grew from 18% to 34%, while electronics from 12% to 30%. A sector-specific approach is needed to support AI adoption The analysis highlights three key components when looking at how firms adopt AI: how much a company has reorganised its way of working to take full advantage of AI, how much it uses AI in production , and to what extent it is adopting ready-to-use AI solutions vs custom made ones, the level of AI commoditisation . Ranking of sectors in key components AI- enhanced organisation, production and AI commoditisation. Source: JRC, based on Eurostat’s survey on ICT usage in enterprises (isoc_e). The ranking of strategic sectors along these key components shows a positive correlation between organisation and production. The firms investing more in structural organisational changes to integrate AI are more likely to use AI in production, suggesting that organisational changes must be prioritised. This is the case of energy, electronic communications or defence industries. The analysis reveals that the use of ready-to-use AI solutions vs custom-made ones depends on the specificities of each sector. For instance, the climate sector, despite having a medium AI uptake, displays a low uptake of off-the-shelf AI solutions, as it requires a higher degree of customisation compared to other strategic sectors. At the same time, the manufacturing sector, overall displaying a low AI uptake, ranks higher than climate for adopting off-the-shelf solutions. This indicates that using accessible ready-to-use AI solutions does not necessarily increase integration of AI into production processes. Overall, the analysis suggests that policy measures aimed at increasing AI integration into core processes need to be tailored to the specificities of the strategic sector. Bottlenecks to AI adoption The data show that the lack of relevant expertise is widely indicated as the main obstacle to AI adoption across the vast majority of strategic sectors. In particular, two factors emerge as the dominant bottlenecks: the scarcity of specialised skills and the regulatory uncertainty, including concerns about data protection and privacy. The report suggests that digitalisation initiatives, skills development, and organisational change can support AI uptake and close the gap between tool uptake to deeper integration. The results of the study will support policy makers with setting targets and create new sector-specific measures on how to increase AI adoption in the strategic economic areas. items.content: Trustworthy AI / Cybersecurity English 한국어 NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform: A Reference for Continuous In-Silicon Agent Monitoring Secure AI agents with a safety enforcement layer spanning software and hardware. Sep 28, 2026 By John Myers , Alex Watson , Ali Golshan and Ofir Arkin Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA OpenShell provides an open-source secure runtime that executes autonomous AI agents in sandboxed environments with kernel-level isolation. The NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform combines OpenShell on NVIDIA Vera CPUs with NVIDIA Sentry on BlueField-4 DPUs to create a layered safety architecture. Five core principles guide the platform: verifiable policy, out-of-band enforcement, controlling the path to the model, scaling agent authority with reasoning visibility, and applying a shared responsibility model across labs, enterprises, and hardware providers. NVIDIA Sentry extends monitoring and enforcement into BlueField hardware using NVIDIA DOCA to correlate agent interactions, policy decisions, and tool access for contextual activity records. In NVIDIA Vera Rubin POD systems, BlueField-4 DPUs sit on the node's only path to the model, providing continuous out-of-band observability and real-time policy enforcement at line speed. Next Steps Get started with NVIDIA OpenShell to run agents in sandboxed environments with kernel-level isolation. Explore the NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform to understand the layered safety architecture for AI agents. Read the technical walkthrough on adding runtime controls to AI agents with NVIDIA OpenShell for implementation details. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more To understand where agentic AI stands today, consider the last seismic shift in technology: the rise of the internet in the 90s. It was new and full of possibilities. You could build a website over a weekend and share it with the world, or chat with someone half way around the world in online chat rooms without long-distance telephone fees. It brought endless opportunity, but also a lot of risk. A website could run code on your machine, steal your sensitive information, or infect your computer with a virus. People loved it anyway. To introduce a layer of trust, the community built things like encrypted connections and a lock icon to know when a connection was safe. The step function change in safety came from a radical security idea at the time: isolate each page in its own sandbox (a tab in a browser) so that a rogue page couldn’t infect the rest of your computer. Amazon, Google, Netflix, and Meta were all built on this trust layer. Security and safety for the internet enabled online commerce, connection, gaming, and so much more that wouldn’t have been possible before. Security and safety didn’t slow the pace of innovation—they allowed it to accelerate. Why build a trusted layer for agents now? Several frontier labs have recently reported versions of the same story: AI agents broke out of the evaluation environments that were meant to contain them and reached systems they never should have been allowed to. Some of the agents even misreported what they did. The security controls in place were insufficient. Over the past few weeks, these reports have led to a serious debate about the pace of agent development. We believe we need to increase the pace of AI safety research and engineering in collaboration with frontier labs and the broader community. It was not a single new capability that led to these breakouts. It was a combination of tools, time, and ambiguous instructions, along with a desire for the agent to think “outside the box.” Agent safety requires independent security controls. The internet was not made secure by requiring that web developers promise to be good. It became safe because the browser stopped trusting the code in the web pages explicitly. We need to build this trust layer for agents. Figure 1. NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform Reference Design combines NVIDIA OpenShell on NVIDIA Vera and NVIDIA Sentry on NVIDIA BlueField-4 Lessons learned from building OpenShell NVIDIA OpenShell (Apache 2.0) is an open source secure runtime for executing autonomous AI agents in sandboxed environments with kernel-level isolation. Building OpenShell over the past year, we have learned that every agent should run in a zero-trust environment out of the box. They need isolation, monitoring, and behavior detection. Today, we are introducing an open stack that makes this possible. In our own research, we’ve watched how agents can go off course. Drift refers to agent actions that depart from the intended task or operating constraints. Drift can occur in response to a policy block, a bug, or a missing tool. Drift can also occur when instructions are ambiguous or agents are left to run for days or weeks to solve hard problems where the first 1,000 things they try do not work. This can’t be trained away while retaining the capability. And here’s the most important lesson: an agent in these circumstances cannot be expected to fully govern its own behavior. Five core principles for building an agent system Policy needs to be verifiable: Before an agent runs, a prover shows that its policy cannot escape the intent of the operator. Enforcement must be out of band: The controls do not live inside, or within reach of the agent. The agent does not need to know it is being watched. The path to the model (the brain) is the control point: An agent cannot act without its next thought. By controlling the path to the model, you own both the best observation point and also the kill switch to interrupt it if you need to. Scale agent authority with the ability to inspect its thinking: The more an agent can do, the more its reasoning needs to be visible. An advantage of open models is that the entire reasoning space and activations are all visible. Applying the shared responsibility model: Labs, enterprises, and hardware providers each own a layer, just like the cloud today. The agent runtime and its policy language need to be open so any provider can plug in. Three open agent safety platform layers A safety platform for AI agents includes the following three layers: The application: What end-users are building. Contains the necessary primitives for mission success: models, harnesses, tools, data, and support scripts and programs. The runtime: Projects the application layer onto infrastructure. Orchestrates the agentic workload onto infrastructure that meets end-user requirements (end-user workstation, edge device, data center) and provides continuous monitoring and real-time policy enforcement and governance. The infrastructure: Concrete hardware resources used to execute agentic workloads. items.content: Back to Articles One Model Family, Two Gold-Level Results: Fine-Tuning Nemotron for IOI and IMO Enterprise + Article Published October 7, 2026 Upvote 24 +18 Aleksander aficek Follow nvidia Igor Gitman igitman Follow nvidia Sean Narenthiran SeanNaren Follow nvidia Mehrzad Samadi mehrzads Follow nvidia Somshubra Majumdar smajumdar94 Follow nvidia The International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) and the International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) test different skills. IOI requires algorithms and code that pass hidden tests under strict time and submission limits. IMO demands rigorous natural-language proofs. Success at either competition is difficult. Success at both points to something broader. Our recent results show that Nemotron is a strong, adaptable foundation for building world-class specialist models. Starting from Nemotron 3, our teams used supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning (RL), and feedback-driven inference to create systems that reached gold-medal level at both IMO 2026 and IOI 2026 . Competition Nemotron specialization Result IOI 2026 Nemotron-3-Ultra-CC with SFT and GenCorrect 535.4/600, above the 361.12 gold threshold and the top human score of 498.27 IMO 2026 Nemotron 3 Ultra general, SFT, and RL checkpoints in a generate-verify-refine system 30/42, above the official gold threshold of 29 The IOI result came from a live, prospective run under the same time, internet-access, and submission constraints as human contestants. It was an unofficial, unsupervised benchmark and was not included in the official IOI ranking. The IMO system’s submitted proofs were graded by official IMO graders. A reusable specialization recipe "Easy to fine-tune" should mean more than making a checkpoint trainable. It should mean that a capable foundation model can be adapted to a demanding domain with a clear, reusable recipe. Across the two projects, that recipe had four parts: Start with a strong Nemotron base model. Curate domain-specific problems and high-quality reasoning traces. Apply standard post-training methods such as SFT and, where useful, RL. Pair the specialist model with an inference loop that generates, evaluates, and improves candidate answers. The training and inference runs were substantial, but the underlying approach is familiar and reproducible. We did not need to build a new foundation model for every challenge. We specialized Nemotron for the task. From general coding ability to IOI gold For competitive programming, we curated 22,000 problems and generated synthetic reasoning traces to train two specialists. Nemotron-3-Nano-CC, with 30 billion total parameters and 3 billion active parameters, received both SFT and RL. Nemotron-3-Ultra-CC, with 550 billion total parameters and 55 billion active parameters, received SFT. The progression on IOI 2025 makes the value of specialization easy to see. Nano improved from 130 points before post-training to 280 after SFT and 291 after RL. With GenCorrect, our iterative generate-evaluate-refine strategy, it reached 468 points and crossed the gold threshold of 438.3. Ultra-CC reached 502 points with the same test-time strategy. These experiments also showed that adaptation does not have to look the same at every scale. SFT produced most of Nano's gain, with RL adding a smaller but consistent improvement. For the stronger Ultra model, one SFT epoch was enough to outperform the fully post-trained Nano model across IOI, ICPC, and LiveCodeBench Pro. That finding guided the competition-specific Ultra-CC system used for IOI 2026, which scored 535.4 out of 600. Teaching Nemotron to prove, check, and revise The IMO project applied the same idea to olympiad mathematics. Starting from Nemotron 3 Ultra, we trained one specialist with SFT and another with RL. The SFT corpus contained 414,890 quality-filtered examples across 15,818 unique proof problems. It did more than teach final answers. The data covered proof generation, refinement, verification, and meta-verification, so the model learned to construct arguments, identify gaps, respond to critiques, and judge whether a proof was complete. The RL model was trained on 9,597 proof problems selected near the model's capability frontier. Both post-trained checkpoints outperformed the general-availability model in the development experiments. The SFT checkpoint was strongest in the first search round, while the RL checkpoint achieved the best overall single-checkpoint result. Their strengths were complementary, so the final system used both specialists alongside the general model. For each IMO problem, the models generated candidate proofs, scored them, produced critiques, and refined the most promising attempts. A separate high-compute stage selected the final submission. The entire system worked in natural language, with no formal prover, external tools, or internet access. It scored 30 out of 42 points, including full credit on four of the six problems, and exceeded the official gold-medal threshold. Fine-tuning and test-time compute work together Our earlier IOI 2025 Hugging Face post showed how test-time compute can push open-weight models to gold-level performance. The new results add an important piece: better specialization gives the inference system better candidates, better critics, and better refinements. At IOI, GenCorrect turned the gains from fine-tuning into larger improvements over multiple feedback rounds. At IMO, using complementary SFT and RL checkpoints was more valuable than simply drawing more samples from one checkpoint. In both cases, the best outcome came from combining a capable specialist with a system that could search, verify, and improve. This distinction matters. The medals were not produced by fine-tuning alone, and they were not produced by brute-force sampling alone. They came from co-designing the model, the data, and the inference loop. Open models, data, and recipes on Hugging Face We want these results to be useful beyond the competitions. The Nemotron Labs IMO 2026 collection brings together the SFT and RL checkpoints, both training datasets, and Nemotron-IMO-Bench, a new benchmark of 200 olympiad-level problems. The IMO paper describes the training approach and generate-verify-refine system, while the NeMo-Skills repository includes the IMO inference pipeline, prompts, submitted proofs, and a reproducible quickstart. For competitive programming, the Nemotron-3-Ultra-CC model is available on Hugging Face, and the IOI paper provides the training recipe and the GenCorrect methodology. The IOI evaluation and inference pipeline are also available in NeMo-Skills . Together, IMO and IOI provide unusually demanding evidence for a simple idea: Nemotron can be fine-tuned into world-class domain specialists, then composed with transparent inference workflows to solve problems at the frontier of human competition. We are excited to see what the Hugging Face community builds next. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.18838 (cs) [Submitted on 13 Oct 2026] Title: Scaling Online Optimal Transport Minibatches for Flow Matching Authors: Peter Chen , Sergey Levine View a PDF of the paper titled Scaling Online Optimal Transport Minibatches for Flow Matching, by Peter Chen and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: A central challenge in scaling flow models is maintaining stability in training and integration. In flow matching, this stability depends critically on how source samples are paired with data. Independent random pairing introduces substantial stochasticity, motivating minibatch optimal transport (OT) to construct online source-target couplings that reduce this randomness (Tong et al., 2024). However, as applications extend to larger and higher-dimensional datasets, small minibatches can limit these benefits, while scaling the coupling to substantially larger minibatches at every iteration is computationally prohibitive. Moreover, how OT coupling affects the full stochastic gradient and integration remains theoretically unresolved. In this work, we develop a scalable online entropic OT approximation that enables substantially larger source-target couplings while preserving the benefits of OT. We close the theoretical gap for both unregularized and entropic OT by proving strict reductions in full stochastic-gradient variance and integration error relative to independent pairing, and further characterize how these improvements strengthen as the online coupling minibatch grows. Experiments on single-cell gene interpolation-flow and image-flow training validate these predictions, showing that larger online couplings consistently improve training stability and final generation performance. Scaling Online Optimal Transport Minibatches for Flow Matching Peter Chen Sergey Levine Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley Abstract A central challenge in scaling flow models is maintaining stability in training and integration. In flow matching, this stability depends critically on how source samples are paired with data. Independent random pairing introduces substantial stochasticity, motivating minibatch optimal transport (OT) to construct online source-target couplings that reduce this randomness ( Tong et al., 2024 ) . However, as applications extend to larger and higher-dimensional datasets, small minibatches can limit these benefits, while scaling the coupling to substantially larger minibatches at every iteration is computationally prohibitive. Moreover, how OT coupling affects the full stochastic gradient and integration remains theoretically unresolved. In this work, we develop a scalable online entropic OT approximation that enables substantially larger source-target couplings while preserving the benefits of OT. We close the theoretical gap for both unregularized and entropic OT by proving strict reductions in full stochastic-gradient variance and integration error relative to independent pairing, and further characterize how these improvements strengthen as the online coupling minibatch grows. Experiments on single-cell gene interpolation-flow and image-flow training validate these predictions, showing that larger online couplings consistently improve training stability and final generation performance. 1 Introduction Much of the recent progress in generative AI has been driven by scale. Autoregressive language models benefit from a standardized learning objective: next-token prediction under a softmax distribution. Once this objective is fixed, much of the challenge of scaling shifts to systems and optimization. Flow models introduce an additional dimension: their supervision is constructed along a generative path from noise to data, and the resulting regression targets depend on how source noise samples are coupled with target data samples. Thus, scaling flow models requires consideration not only of how the model is optimized, but also of how its training targets are constructed. The choice of such source-target coupling is therefore part of the learning problem itself. In flow matching, each training example pairs a source sample from the noise distribution with a target data sample and regresses the velocity along the resulting interpolation path. Under the standard independent coupling, these pairings are random. Consequently, nearby intermediate states can arise from different endpoint pairs and receive substantially different velocity targets, increasing ambiguity in the regression problem and the variance of stochastic gradients. A natural way to reduce this randomness is to determine the source-target correspondence during training. Optimal transport (OT) then provides a natural solution by constructing a coupling between source and target samples within each minibatch during training. Such online coupling minimizes the transport cost between the two empirical distributions, yielding more coherent source-target assignments that induce straighter flows and reduce the ambiguity of independent pairing ( Pooladian et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) . However, as flow matching is applied to larger and more heterogeneous datasets, such as high-dimensional single-cell trajectories and large-scale image datasets, a fixed small coupling minibatch can become increasingly restrictive, where each minibatch only exposes OT to a limited subset of the source and target distributions, constraining the candidate correspondences available at each iteration. As the underlying data distribution grows in diversity and complexity, it therefore becomes natural to scale the OT minibatch accordingly. Still, scaling the minibatch size is computationally challenging, where dense pairwise interactions in standard OT restrict practical minibatches to hundreds of samples. Nevertheless, recent advances in scalable entropic OT make substantially larger contexts accessible. In particular, FlashSinkhorn ( Ye et al., 2026 ) implements Sinkhorn iterations with FlashAttention-style HBM kernels without materializing the full coupling matrix in high-bandwidth memory. To this end, we propose a simple, tractable approximation by replacing online OT coupling with scalable entropic OT, enabling coupling contexts to grow from hundreds to thousands of samples during training. The price of this tractability is that entropic regularization changes the coupling itself. The regularization strength ε \varepsilon controls this deviation from standard OT, while the minibatch size k k controls the scale of the online coupling. Understanding whether the stability benefits of OT persist therefore requires characterizing the joint effects of regularization and coupling scale. Moreover, this question remains unresolved even for standard unregularized minibatch OT. Existing analyses motivate OT through straighter paths and reduced conditional uncertainty ( Pooladian et al., 2023 ; Boïté et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Chambolle and Hertrich, 2026 ) , but do not provide a general strict characterization of its effect on the full stochastic-gradient variance or the induced numerical integration error. By making larger online couplings feasible, we determine whether their stability benefits survive the approximation required for scaling. Our contributions can be summarized below: Contributions. We provide a unified and principled characterization of how online OT coupling affects optimization and numerical integration. On the optimization side, we characterize the full stochastic-gradient variance by (i) proving that population quadratic OT strictly reduces this variance relative to independent coupling, (ii) showing that unregularized minibatch-OT variance reduces as the minibatch size k k grows, and (iii) extending same guarantees to entropic-regularized couplings. On the integration side, we establish parallel strict reductions in Euler integration error and characterize how these guarantees improve with scaled minibatch size. These results provide a better theoretical understanding for using and scaling entropic OT as a replacement to the standard online OT couplings. Related works. OT-based conditional flow matching (OT-CFM) improves both training and generation through better source-target pairings ( Tong et al., 2024 ; Pooladian et al., 2023 ) . Given the difficulty to scale OT-CFM, recent works scale the minibatch context by separating pairing from training: Zhang et al. (2026) precomputed million-scale couplings offline, which requires buffering enough pairs to cover the entire training run before optimization begins; semidiscrete approximation methods offer better efficiency by reusing fitted dataset-level potentials, but need a separate potential-optimization stage ( Mousavi-Hosseini et al., 2026 ) or face non-convergence when scaled to large unconditional datasets ( Kong et al., 2026 ) . Therefore, we return to the original challenge, by finding an affordable and stable method for scaling the minibatch that flow matching recomputes from fresh samples at every training iteration. The existing theory has so far addressed separate pieces. Tong et al. (2024) connect population OT to dynamic OT, while Pooladian et al. (2023) study conditional gradient covariance and asymptotic BatchOT straightness. Finite-batch theory remains limited: Zhang et al. (2026) characterize uncertainty in the resulting OT coupling, while Boïté et al. (2026) analyze its integration benefit only in a restricted two-atom model; more recent work also studies full parameter-gradient variance in restricted Gaussian models ( Reu et al., 2025 ) and integration error through the geometry of a prescribed velocity field ( Tao and Choi, 2026 ) . Thus, no prior result establishes that replacing independent pairing with minibatch OT strictly reduces full stochastic-gradient variance while inducing a general integration advantage; we defer further related work to Appendix A . 2 Preliminaries We introduce flow matching (FM) and coupling definitions used throughout the later analyses. Scaling Online Optimal Transport Minibatches for Flow Matching Peter Chen Sergey Levine Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley Abstract A central challenge in scaling flow models is maintaining stability in training and integration. In flow matching, this stability depends critically on how source samples are paired with data. Independent random pairing introduces substantial stochasticity, motivating minibatch optimal transport (OT) to construct online source-target couplings that reduce this randomness ( Tong et al., 2024 ) . However, as applications extend to larger and higher-dimensional datasets, small minibatches can limit these benefits, while scaling the coupling to substantially larger minibatches at every iteration is computationally prohibitive. Moreover, how OT coupling affects the full stochastic gradient and integration remains theoretically unresolved. In this work, we develop a scalable online entropic OT approximation that enables substantially larger source-target couplings while preserving the benefits of OT. We close the theoretical gap for both unregularized and entropic OT by proving strict reductions in full stochastic-gradient variance and integration error relative to independent pairing, and further characterize how these improvements strengthen as the online coupling minibatch grows. Experiments on single-cell gene interpolation-flow and image-flow training validate these predictions, showing that larger online couplings consistently improve training stability and final generation performance. 1 Introduction Much of the recent progress in generative AI has been driven by scale. Autoregressive language models benefit from a standardized learning objective: next-token prediction under a softmax distribution. Once this objective is fixed, much of the challenge of scaling shifts to systems and optimization. Flow models introduce an additional dimension: their supervision is constructed along a generative path from noise to data, and the resulting regression targets depend on how source noise samples are coupled with target data samples. Thus, scaling flow models requires consideration not only of how the model is optimized, but also of how its training targets are constructed. The choice of such source-target coupling is therefore part of the learning problem itself. In flow matching, each training example pairs a source sample from the noise distribution with a target data sample and regresses the velocity along the resulting interpolation path. Under the standard independent coupling, these pairings are random. Consequently, nearby intermediate states can arise from different endpoint pairs and receive substantially different velocity targets, increasing ambiguity in the regression problem and the variance of stochastic gradients. A natural way to reduce this randomness is to determine the source-target correspondence during training. Optimal transport (OT) then provides a natural solution by constructing a coupling between source and target samples within each minibatch during training. Such online coupling minimizes the transport cost between the two empirical distributions, yielding more coherent source-target assignments that induce straighter flows and reduce the ambiguity of independent pairing ( Pooladian et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) . However, as flow matching is applied to larger and more heterogeneous datasets, such as high-dimensional single-cell trajectories and large-scale image datasets, a fixed small coupling minibatch can become increasingly restrictive, where each minibatch only exposes OT to a limited subset of the source and target distributions, constraining the candidate correspondences available at each iteration. As the underlying data distribution grows in diversity and complexity, it therefore becomes natural to scale the OT minibatch accordingly. Still, scaling the minibatch size is computationally challenging, where dense pairwise interactions in standard OT restrict practical minibatches to hundreds of samples. Nevertheless, recent advances in scalable entropic OT make substantially larger contexts accessible. In particular, FlashSinkhorn ( Ye et al., 2026 ) implements Sinkhorn iterations with FlashAttention-style HBM kernels without materializing the full coupling matrix in high-bandwidth memory. To this end, we propose a simple, tractable approximation by replacing online OT coupling with scalable entropic OT, enabling coupling contexts to grow from hundreds to thousands of samples during training. The price of this tractability is that entropic regularization changes the coupling itself. The regularization strength ε \varepsilon controls this deviation from standard OT, while the minibatch size k k controls the scale of the online coupling. Understanding whether the stability benefits of OT persist therefore requires characterizing the joint effects of regularization and coupling scale. Moreover, this question remains unresolved even for standard unregularized minibatch OT. Existing analyses motivate OT through straighter paths and reduced conditional uncertainty ( Pooladian et al., 2023 ; Boïté et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Chambolle and Hertrich, 2026 ) , but do not provide a general strict characterization of its effect on the full stochastic-gradient variance or the induced numerical integration error. By making larger online couplings feasible, we determine whether their stability benefits survive the approximation required for scaling. Our contributions can be summarized below: Contributions. We provide a unified and principled characterization of how online OT coupling affects optimization and numerical integration. On the optimization side, we characterize the full stochastic-gradient variance by (i) proving that population quadratic OT strictly reduces this variance relative to independent coupling, (ii) showing that unregularized minibatch-OT variance reduces as the minibatch size k k grows, and (iii) extending same guarantees to entropic-regularized couplings. On the integration side, we establish parallel strict reductions in Euler integration error and characterize how these guarantees improve with scaled minibatch size. These results provide a better theoretical understanding for using and scaling entropic OT as a replacement to the standard online OT couplings. Related works. OT-based conditional flow matching (OT-CFM) improves both training and generation through better source-target pairings ( Tong et al., 2024 ; Pooladian et al., 2023 ) . Given the difficulty to scale OT-CFM, recent works scale the minibatch context by separating pairing from training: Zhang et al. (2026) precomputed million-scale couplings offline, which requires buffering enough pairs to cover the entire training run before optimization begins; semidiscrete approximation methods offer better efficiency by reusing fitted dataset-level potentials, but need a separate potential-optimization stage ( Mousavi-Hosseini et al., 2026 ) or face non-convergence when scaled to large unconditional datasets ( Kong et al., 2026 ) . Therefore, we return to the original challenge, by finding an affordable and stable method for scaling the minibatch that flow matching recomputes from fresh samples at every training iteration. The existing theory has so far addressed separate pieces. Tong et al. (2024) connect population OT to dynamic OT, while Pooladian et al. (2023) study conditional gradient covariance and asymptotic BatchOT straightness. Finite-batch theory remains limited: Zhang et al. (2026) characterize uncertainty in the resulting OT coupling, while Boïté et al. (2026) analyze its integration benefit only in a restricted two-atom model; more recent work also studies full parameter-gradient variance in restricted Gaussian models ( Reu et al., 2025 ) and integration error through the geometry of a prescribed velocity field ( Tao and Choi, 2026 ) . Thus, no prior result establishes that replacing independent pairing with minibatch OT strictly reduces full stochastic-gradient variance while inducing a general integration advantage; we defer further related work to Appendix A . 2 Preliminaries We introduce flow matching (FM) and coupling definitions used throughout the later analyses. items.title: Digital Talent EU Days 2026: Building the skills for Europe's digital future
items.summary: Digital Talent EU Days 2026 will explore how Europe can close digital skills gaps and strengthen its competitiveness. items.content: Digital Talent EU Days 2026 will explore how Europe can close digital skills gaps and strengthen its competitiveness. LEADSx2030 and Connecting Women in Digital On 15 and 16 October, the Digital Talent EU Days 2026 will bring together policymakers, industry representatives, educators and digital skills experts at Trinity Business School, Trinity College Dublin, to discuss one of Europe's most pressing challenges: developing, attracting and retaining the talent needed for a competitive, secure digital future. Organised by LEADSx2030 and Connecting Women in Digital , in partnership with the European Commission and other stakeholders, the event takes place alongside the European AI Innovation Month , at a time when Europe is accelerating efforts to bring artificial intelligence from the screen into the real economy and society. Skills and talent are at the heart of this transformation , and as AI reshapes industries and professions, Europe needs a workforce capable not only of developing advanced technologies, but also of integrating and applying them effectively. This includes strengthening capabilities in AI, cybersecurity and other strategic digital areas that are essential to Europe's competitiveness, resilience and technological sovereignty. Discussions will focus on three interconnected priorities: Closing digital skills gaps; Expanding participation in the digital workforce, particularly among women and underrepresented groups; Turning policy ambitions into practical action through stronger cooperation between businesses, education providers and public authorities. The event will also explore how upskilling, reskilling and emerging skills pathways can respond to changing labour market needs, while ensuring that women play a stronger role in designing, developing and leading Europe's digital transformation. Through workshops, debates and exchanges of good practices, the Digital Talent EU Days will provide an opportunity to connect initiatives, share lessons learned and identify practical approaches to building Europe's digital talent pipeline. Last update 14 October 2026 Print as PDF

items.title: Make America Healthy Again
items.summary: Make america healthy again President Trump launched the Make America Healthy Again initiative to confront chronic disease, improve nutrition, and lower healthcare costs. This year, the administration advanced reforms targeting childhood health, food quality, and preventive care while increasing transparency and accountability in healthcare systems. These actions are laying the foundation for a healthier, stronger America. By prioritizing prevention over treatment and empowering families with better information and choices, the administration is addressing the root causes of poor health outcomes. These efforts are improving quality of life, strengthening communities, and ensuring a healthier future for the next generation of Americans. Eisenhower presidential actions Establishment of a Committee of Inquiry to Investigate Allegations of False Statements by Lisa DeNell Cook October 7, 2026 Read more : Establishment of a Committee of Inquiry to Investigate Allegations of False Statements by Lisa DeNell Cook promises made, promises kept 01 The Trump administration made incredible strides in its effort to Make America Healthy Again, with roughly 35% of the American food industry — including major corporations like Walmart, Hershey and Nestlé — agreeing to eliminate artificial dyes from their products. 02 At President Trump’s direction, the Department of Health and Human Services revised its childhood vaccine recommendations from 72 shots for 11 diseases to 10 “consensus vaccines.” 03 President Trump established the Make America Healthy Again Commission, tasked with investigating and addressing the root causes of America’s escalating health crisis, with an initial focus on childhood chronic diseases. 04 Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins signed a slew of waivers allowing states to remove junk food from SNAP. 05 The Department of Health and Human Services removed COVID-19 vaccines from the list of shots recommended for healthy children and pregnant women. 06 Following negotiations with the Trump Administration, a variety of major pharmaceutical companies have agreed to bring American drug prices in line with the lowest paid by other developed nations, ending decades of Big Pharma exploiting U.S. consumers. 07 President Trump secured $50 billion in funding for rural hospitals. 08 President Trump signed the Whole Milk for Health Kids Act into law, restoring nutritious whole and 2% milk in American schools. 09 The Trump Administration Rollins released new dietary guidelines that prioritize whole, nutrient-dense foods over processed junk. items.content: NVIDIA and Semiconductor Leaders Advance AI Across Chip Design and Manufacturing for AI-Defined Fabs October 14, 2026 News Summary: NVIDIA introduces cuPotential, a new NVIDIA CUDA-X library developers can use to build AI agents that simulate how atoms and molecules interact, accelerating already GPU-optimized workflows by an additional 2-3x in early-access testing. NanoVDB, an open source library for working with 3D data, accelerates chipmaking simulation for AI-defined fabs, helping Lam Research achieve 30x faster simulation. NVIDIA NPP, a library for processing images on GPUs, accelerates chipmaking inspection for AI-defined fabs, helping KLA accelerate inspection. Applied Materials, Cadence, KLA, Lam Research, Siemens, Synopsys and other semiconductor leaders are using NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AI stack across chip design, manufacturing and testing, helping drive faster development, better yield and greater production capacity. NVIDIA today announced semiconductor leaders are adopting NVIDIA CUDA-X ™ libraries — including the new NVIDIA cuPotential library, which developers can use to build AI agents that simulate how atoms and molecules interact — to advance AI-defined fabs. AI-defined fabs are semiconductor factories where AI helps engineers optimize processes, solve production issues and improve production efficiency. As demand for advanced chips rises, such fabs must expand production while managing increasingly complex manufacturing processes. Engineers need new ways to model materials, analyze inspection data and test process changes in digital twins before applying them in production. The expanded CUDA-X portfolio gives AI agents and engineering applications accelerated tools for semiconductor simulation, 3D data processing and image analysis, helping automate more engineering work across chip design and manufacturing so fabs can predict process behavior and improve yield. “The semiconductor industry made the AI revolution possible. Now, AI is transforming how chips are built,” said Tim Costa, vice president and general manager of industrial and computational engineering at NVIDIA. “As fabs race to meet demand for advanced chips, NVIDIA CUDA-X and Omniverse libraries give AI agents accelerated simulation and inspection tools to help engineers manage complexity, improve yield and advance AI-defined fabs.” NVIDIA cuPotential Accelerates How Researchers Model Atomic Interactions Understanding how atoms and molecules interact is critical to modeling semiconductor materials and manufacturing processes, but these calculations can take significant amounts of time, even in software already optimized for GPUs. NVIDIA cuPotential accelerates atomic-scale simulation with specialized GPU-accelerated functions developers can add to existing software. It helps researchers model electrical forces and other interactions across large numbers of atoms to test and refine simulations faster. Synopsys is among the early adopters using cuPotential to accelerate materials simulations. By making these modeling capabilities available to AI agents, cuPotential helps agents run, evaluate and iterate on advanced molecular simulations. In early-access testing, the library accelerated already GPU-optimized workflows by an additional 2-3x. Semiconductor Leaders Advance AI-Defined Fabs With NVIDIA CUDA-X AI-defined fabs require faster ways to model chip designs, materials behavior and manufacturing processes before changes reach production. NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries — including NVIDIA cuPotential for simulating atomic interactions, NVIDIA cuEST for modeling electronic behavior and NVIDIA cuDSS for solving complex engineering simulations — accelerate these workloads to help make fabs more autonomous. Synopsys is using cuPotential, cuEST and cuDSS to accelerate semiconductor simulations, with early QuantumATK results showing a potential 30x speedup using cuEST, and S-Device benchmarks showing a 12x speedup using cuDSS. The company’s AgentEngineer solutions interoperate with NVIDIA Nemotron ™ open models and NVIDIA NeMo ™ to support AI agents for chip design and verification. Cadence is using NVIDIA accelerated computing, NVIDIA Nemotron open models and CUDA-X libraries to bring agentic AI to the design and simulation of electromechanical systems — from semiconductors to advanced packaging and printed circuit boards. Examples include Cadence AuraStack AI Super Agent optimizing advanced packages for heat and stress 8x faster using cuDSS with Cadence Celsius, and Nemotron with ChipStack AI Super Agent for semiconductor design and verification. COMSOL is accelerating semiconductor multiphysics simulations with NVIDIA cuDSS, delivering up to 10x faster simulations to help engineers optimize equipment and processes. Its upcoming COMSOL MCP Server will use the NVIDIA Nemotron Ultra open model to enable AI-assisted modeling and design exploration. Voltai accelerates advanced chip packaging with Voltaire, its agentic multiphysics platform for 3D-IC design and simulation. Voltaire combines AI agents with GPU-accelerated solvers powered by NVIDIA cuDSS and CUDA-X libraries, compressing complex electro-thermal-mechanical simulation workflows from months to a day. ChipAgents uses NVIDIA AI infrastructure and NVIDIA model-training and optimization software to develop specialized AI models for chip design. The company is also working with NVIDIA to develop Build-A-Chip Bench , a new AI benchmark that evaluates agents across end-to-end workflows from specification to graphic data system. The benchmark gives the industry a comprehensive measure of progress toward fully autonomous semiconductor engineering. NVIDIA Open Libraries Help Prepare and Optimize Manufacturing Workflows Fabs depend on thousands of process steps that must be modeled, refined and validated before production. The NVIDIA cuLitho library accelerates calculations for printing chip patterns; NanoVDB — an open source library for working with 3D data — accelerates chipmaking simulations; and the open NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo ™ framework helps train physics AI models to predict how physical systems behave. Siemens is using cuLitho to speed up Calibre software for chip-pattern refinement and mask preparation. Its Solido team is also developing agent-driven characterization workflows with Nemotron open models and NVIDIA NeMo open libraries. Lam Research intends to integrate NanoVDB into its advanced semiconductor process modeling platform SEMulator3D , part of the company’s Semiverse Solutions family of virtual products. The addition of NanoVDB is expected to accelerate select wafer-etch modeling by up to 30x, while using NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo has been demonstrated to assist in reducing plasma-prediction simulation time to as little as milliseconds instead of days. Luminary is applying NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo to semiconductor package design, training physics AI models to predict temperature, pressure drop and thermal stress across package configurations — enabling engineers to explore 100x more designs in the same schedule without running a new simulation for every option. AI-Defined Fabs Inspect and Test Chips With NVIDIA CUDA-X Libraries AI-defined fabs need to analyze inspection images and test data quickly enough to catch defects, maintain equipment and improve yield. NVIDIA NPP, a library for processing images on GPUs, and NVIDIA RAPIDS cuDF, a library for processing large datasets on GPUs, help accelerate test and quality-control workflows. Using NVIDIA AI and accelerated computing, imec is removing noise from scanning electron microscope images used for sub-nanometer chip measurements and using NVIDIA cuLitho to enable computationally intensive process-window optical proximity correction — achieving a 30% improvement in the lithography process window. KLA applied insights from its highly optimized production kernels to a new NPP NCC kernel that achieved performance levels 50x faster than earlier CPU versions, comparable with KLA’s hand-tuned implementations. Teradyne is using NVIDIA NPP and accelerated computing to accelerate image-sensor testing, and RAPIDS cuDF and CuPy for GPU calculations, to deliver approximately 85x faster probe-maintenance inference, helping identify degrading probes before they affect yield. Advantest has integrated NVIDIA Nemotron and NVIDIA Kumo-Anomaly into ACS RTDI to enable AI-driven semiconductor production analytics. Powered by NVIDIA Grace Blackwell systems, ACS delivers real-time diagnostics and inferencing that recommend corrective actions for test cells. Advantest is also using NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard AI agents to automate model selection, streamline semiconductor test workflows and reduce response times from hours to minutes. NVIDIA Technologies Advance Fab Operations and Automation In an AI-defined fab, equipment data must move from instruments into AI systems fast enough to support operational decisions. Applied Materials is using NVIDIA Omniverse™ and NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including cuDSS, cuEST and PhysicsNeMo, across materials discovery, process development and fab optimization — enabling up to 35x faster chamber simulations and fab digital twins that help optimize layouts and material flow. Analog Devices Inc. is combining Synopsys physics simulation with the NVIDIA Isaac Sim™ framework and Omniverse libraries to develop high-fidelity sensing simulations and robotic benchmarks, helping engineers evaluate how sensors behave within complete robotic systems. FANUC and Foxconn are connecting their robot models to the Mega NVIDIA Omniverse Blueprint, enabling manufacturers to simulate and validate robotic operations in factory digital twins before physical deployment. OMRON is using NVIDIA Cosmos™ open world models and the NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization in its inspection equipment to develop agents that combine visual data, equipment documentation and manufacturing knowledge. These agents help engineers analyze printed circuit board results, investigate potential defect causes, and support troubleshooting and quality control. Availability NVIDIA cuPotential is available in early access. NanoVDB is available as open source within OpenVDB, and NPP is available through NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit . Lam Research’s NanoVDB-accelerated SEMulator3D capability is targeted for release by the end of this year. Learn more by joining NVIDIA at SEMICON West . items.raw_text: NVIDIA and Semiconductor Leaders Advance AI Across Chip Design and Manufacturing for AI-Defined Fabs October 14, 2026 News Summary: NVIDIA introduces cuPotential, a new NVIDIA CUDA-X library developers can use to build AI agents that simulate how atoms and molecules interact, accelerating already GPU-optimized workflows by an additional 2-3x in early-access testing. NanoVDB, an open source library for working with 3D data, accelerates chipmaking simulation for AI-defined fabs, helping Lam Research achieve 30x faster simulation. NVIDIA NPP, a library for processing images on GPUs, accelerates chipmaking inspection for AI-defined fabs, helping KLA accelerate inspection. Applied Materials, Cadence, KLA, Lam Research, Siemens, Synopsys and other semiconductor leaders are using NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AI stack across chip design, manufacturing and testing, helping drive faster development, better yield and greater production capacity. NVIDIA today announced semiconductor leaders are adopting NVIDIA CUDA-X ™ libraries — including the new NVIDIA cuPotential library, which developers can use to build AI agents that simulate how atoms and molecules interact — to advance AI-defined fabs. AI-defined fabs are semiconductor factories where AI helps engineers optimize processes, solve production issues and improve production efficiency. As demand for advanced chips rises, such fabs must expand production while managing increasingly complex manufacturing processes. Engineers need new ways to model materials, analyze inspection data and test process changes in digital twins before applying them in production. The expanded CUDA-X portfolio gives AI agents and engineering applications accelerated tools for semiconductor simulation, 3D data processing and image analysis, helping automate more engineering work across chip design and manufacturing so fabs can predict process behavior and improve yield. “The semiconductor industry made the AI revolution possible. Now, AI is transforming how chips are built,” said Tim Costa, vice president and general manager of industrial and computational engineering at NVIDIA. “As fabs race to meet demand for advanced chips, NVIDIA CUDA-X and Omniverse libraries give AI agents accelerated simulation and inspection tools to help engineers manage complexity, improve yield and advance AI-defined fabs.” NVIDIA cuPotential Accelerates How Researchers Model Atomic Interactions Understanding how atoms and molecules interact is critical to modeling semiconductor materials and manufacturing processes, but these calculations can take significant amounts of time, even in software already optimized for GPUs. NVIDIA cuPotential accelerates atomic-scale simulation with specialized GPU-accelerated functions developers can add to existing software. It helps researchers model electrical forces and other interactions across large numbers of atoms to test and refine simulations faster. Synopsys is among the early adopters using cuPotential to accelerate materials simulations. By making these modeling capabilities available to AI agents, cuPotential helps agents run, evaluate and iterate on advanced molecular simulations. In early-access testing, the library accelerated already GPU-optimized workflows by an additional 2-3x. Semiconductor Leaders Advance AI-Defined Fabs With NVIDIA CUDA-X AI-defined fabs require faster ways to model chip designs, materials behavior and manufacturing processes before changes reach production. NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries — including NVIDIA cuPotential for simulating atomic interactions, NVIDIA cuEST for modeling electronic behavior and NVIDIA cuDSS for solving complex engineering simulations — accelerate these workloads to help make fabs more autonomous. Synopsys is using cuPotential, cuEST and cuDSS to accelerate semiconductor simulations, with early QuantumATK results showing a potential 30x speedup using cuEST, and S-Device benchmarks showing a 12x speedup using cuDSS. The company’s AgentEngineer solutions interoperate with NVIDIA Nemotron ™ open models and NVIDIA NeMo ™ to support AI agents for chip design and verification. Cadence is using NVIDIA accelerated computing, NVIDIA Nemotron open models and CUDA-X libraries to bring agentic AI to the design and simulation of electromechanical systems — from semiconductors to advanced packaging and printed circuit boards. Examples include Cadence AuraStack AI Super Agent optimizing advanced packages for heat and stress 8x faster using cuDSS with Cadence Celsius, and Nemotron with ChipStack AI Super Agent for semiconductor design and verification. COMSOL is accelerating semiconductor multiphysics simulations with NVIDIA cuDSS, delivering up to 10x faster simulations to help engineers optimize equipment and processes. Its upcoming COMSOL MCP Server will use the NVIDIA Nemotron Ultra open model to enable AI-assisted modeling and design exploration. Voltai accelerates advanced chip packaging with Voltaire, its agentic multiphysics platform for 3D-IC design and simulation. Voltaire combines AI agents with GPU-accelerated solvers powered by NVIDIA cuDSS and CUDA-X libraries, compressing complex electro-thermal-mechanical simulation workflows from months to a day. ChipAgents uses NVIDIA AI infrastructure and NVIDIA model-training and optimization software to develop specialized AI models for chip design. The company is also working with NVIDIA to develop Build-A-Chip Bench , a new AI benchmark that evaluates agents across end-to-end workflows from specification to graphic data system. The benchmark gives the industry a comprehensive measure of progress toward fully autonomous semiconductor engineering. NVIDIA Open Libraries Help Prepare and Optimize Manufacturing Workflows Fabs depend on thousands of process steps that must be modeled, refined and validated before production. The NVIDIA cuLitho library accelerates calculations for printing chip patterns; NanoVDB — an open source library for working with 3D data — accelerates chipmaking simulations; and the open NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo ™ framework helps train physics AI models to predict how physical systems behave. Siemens is using cuLitho to speed up Calibre software for chip-pattern refinement and mask preparation. Its Solido team is also developing agent-driven characterization workflows with Nemotron open models and NVIDIA NeMo open libraries. Lam Research intends to integrate NanoVDB into its advanced semiconductor process modeling platform SEMulator3D , part of the company’s Semiverse Solutions family of virtual products. The addition of NanoVDB is expected to accelerate select wafer-etch modeling by up to 30x, while using NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo has been demonstrated to assist in reducing plasma-prediction simulation time to as little as milliseconds instead of days. Luminary is applying NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo to semiconductor package design, training physics AI models to predict temperature, pressure drop and thermal stress across package configurations — enabling engineers to explore 100x more designs in the same schedule without running a new simulation for every option. AI-Defined Fabs Inspect and Test Chips With NVIDIA CUDA-X Libraries AI-defined fabs need to analyze inspection images and test data quickly enough to catch defects, maintain equipment and improve yield. NVIDIA NPP, a library for processing images on GPUs, and NVIDIA RAPIDS cuDF, a library for processing large datasets on GPUs, help accelerate test and quality-control workflows. Using NVIDIA AI and accelerated computing, imec is removing noise from scanning electron microscope images used for sub-nanometer chip measurements and using NVIDIA cuLitho to enable computationally intensive process-window optical proximity correction — achieving a 30% improvement in the lithography process window. KLA applied insights from its highly optimized production kernels to a new NPP NCC kernel that achieved performance levels 50x faster than earlier CPU versions, comparable with KLA’s hand-tuned implementations. Teradyne is using NVIDIA NPP and accelerated computing to accelerate image-sensor testing, and RAPIDS cuDF and CuPy for GPU calculations, to deliver approximately 85x faster probe-maintenance inference, helping identify degrading probes before they affect yield. Advantest has integrated NVIDIA Nemotron and NVIDIA Kumo-Anomaly into ACS RTDI to enable AI-driven semiconductor production analytics. Powered by NVIDIA Grace Blackwell systems, ACS delivers real-time diagnostics and inferencing that recommend corrective actions for test cells. Advantest is also using NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard AI agents to automate model selection, streamline semiconductor test workflows and reduce response times from hours to minutes. NVIDIA Technologies Advance Fab Operations and Automation In an AI-defined fab, equipment data must move from instruments into AI systems fast enough to support operational decisions. Applied Materials is using NVIDIA Omniverse™ and NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including cuDSS, cuEST and PhysicsNeMo, across materials discovery, process development and fab optimization — enabling up to 35x faster chamber simulations and fab digital twins that help optimize layouts and material flow. Analog Devices Inc. is combining Synopsys physics simulation with the NVIDIA Isaac Sim™ framework and Omniverse libraries to develop high-fidelity sensing simulations and robotic benchmarks, helping engineers evaluate how sensors behave within complete robotic systems. FANUC and Foxconn are connecting their robot models to the Mega NVIDIA Omniverse Blueprint, enabling manufacturers to simulate and validate robotic operations in factory digital twins before physical deployment. OMRON is using NVIDIA Cosmos™ open world models and the NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization in its inspection equipment to develop agents that combine visual data, equipment documentation and manufacturing knowledge. These agents help engineers analyze printed circuit board results, investigate potential defect causes, and support troubleshooting and quality control. Availability NVIDIA cuPotential is available in early access. NanoVDB is available as open source within OpenVDB, and NPP is available through NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit . Lam Research’s NanoVDB-accelerated SEMulator3D capability is targeted for release by the end of this year. Learn more by joining NVIDIA at SEMICON West . items.title: Offloaded inference for real-world physical AI robotics
