items.content: \tl_set:Ne \mymath mymath Exact Topological Compliance: Generating Persistence-Equivalent Graphs Mattie Ji * Affiliation: University of Pennsylvania Email: mji13@sas.upenn.edu Indradyumna Roy † † thanks: Equal Contributions. Affiliation: Aalto University Email: indradyumna.roy@aalto.fi Vikas Garg Affiliation: YaiYai Ltd & \& Aalto University Email: vgarg@csail.mit.edu Abstract Persistent homology summarizes the topological evolution of a graph as persistence diagrams (PDs). Generating graphs whose topology matches a target descriptor is increasingly important, yet existing topology-aware generative models rely on soft regularization, producing graphs whose PDs may only be approximately similar. We initiate a principled investigation of the generation problem: produce graphs that realize a target PD exactly. We propose two approaches guided by the implicit local and global constraints a target PD imposes. The local approach builds degree-based PD-equivalent graphs iteratively, and we prove that every output realizes the target PD and that every degree-based PD-equivalent graph is reachable. However, as shown thereafter, local generation necessarily trades off between sample diversity and reaching infeasible states. We therefore recast generation as a global constraint satisfaction problem with a complete encoding solvable by modern constraint programming solvers. This is applicable to any vertex-based permutation equivariant filtration scheme and is minimal under the degree filtration. Experiments on four standard graph generation benchmarks confirm that both methods realize the target PD exactly. Together, our methods provide a principled treatment of strict topology-compliant graph generation. Code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/ExactCompliance . 1 Introduction Topological structure is a primary driver of function in many real-world graphs. The presence of components, cycles, and higher-order voids govern stability and catalytic activity in molecules Xia et al. (2015) ; Townsend et al. (2020) ; Wang et al. (2025) , binding affinity and virality Wang et al. (2021) ; Wei (2022) , information flow in brain networks Sizemore et al. (2018) , certain patterns in medical imaging ( Meng et al., 2026 ) , and structural risk in transportation, trade, and infrastructure networks Woldemariam and Attoh-Okine (2025) ; Li et al. (2021) ; Villines (2026) . Persistent homology Carlsson (2009) ; Edelsbrunner and Morozov (2012) is the standard tool for extracting this information. Given a graph G G and a filtration scheme, persistent homology tracks the births and deaths of homological features along the induced subgraph sequence. The result is a multiset of pairs ( b , d ) (b,d) called the persistence diagram (PD). PDs are stable under perturbation ( Cohen-Steiner et al., 2006 ) , computable with efficient algorithms ( Otter et al., 2017 ) , and have become the workhorse of topological data analysis (TDA) in machine learning, underpinning almost every topology-aware approach to graph and higher-order neural networks ( Hofer et al., 2020 ; Immonen et al., 2023 ; Ballester and Rieck, 2025 ; Horn et al., 2021 ; Ji et al., 2025a ; Ji et al., 2026 ; Yan et al., 2022 ; Carriere et al., 2020 ; Russold and Kerber, 2024 ; Verma et al., 2024 ; Papamarkou et al., 2024 ) and providing topological signals that standard message passing alone cannot recover (e.g., cycle detection). In parallel, graph generation has recently emerged as a central tool across these same domains, with autoregressive ( You et al., 2018 ) , one-shot ( Simonovsky and Komodakis, 2018 ) , and diffusion-based ( Niu et al., 2020 ; Jo et al., 2022 ; Vignac et al., 2022 ) models. Recent work conditions generation on domain-specific structural properties: spectral profile ( Martinkus et al., 2022 ) , molecular validity ( De Cao and Kipf, 2018 ; Jin et al., 2020 ) , and structural constraints like planarity and acyclicity ( Madeira et al., 2024 ) . Conditioning on topology is a natural next step, but largely unexplored. A recent attempt Park et al. (2025) , augments discrete diffusion with a 1 1 -Wasserstein PD-matching loss. This soft regularizer nudges the learned distribution toward topological plausibility, but offers no guarantees that individually generated graphs attain the desired topological structure (e.g., the target number of cycles and components). Table 1: Overview of the core contributions in our paper. Local Generation of PD-Equivalent Filtrations (Section 3 ) Local Generation for General/Vertex/Degree Filtrations Algorithm 1 , 2 , 3 Correctness and Diversity of Local Generations Theorem 3.1 , 3.7 , 3.9 Perfect Generation on Acyclic Graphs (for General/Vertex) Corollary 3.4 , 3.8 Impossibility Results for Local Generation Theorem 3.10 Global Generation of PD-Equivalent Graphs (Section 4 ) Global Generation for Any Canonical Vertex Filtration Scheme Φ \Phi Section 4.1 Soundness, Completeness, and Degree Minimality of Encoding Theorem 4.2 Experiments (Section 5 ) Local vs. Global on Four Graph Generation Benchmarks Table 2 Comparison Against PD-Conditioned Neural Diffusion Baselines Table 3 , Figure 3 PD-conditioned graph generation from first principles. A PD is a finite summary of an underlying combinatorial structure and therefore collapses many graphs to the same image. The most widely studied filtration scheme in the graph learning literature is the vertex-degree function Ballester and Rieck (2025) ; Horn et al. (2021) ; Park et al. (2025) ; Yan et al. (2022) ; Hofer et al. (2020) ; Hofer et al. (2017) : it is permutation-equivariant and aligns naturally with the local message-passing inductive bias of GNNs. We adopt it as the primary filtration scheme throughout this paper and discuss extensions to other vertex-based, permutation-equivariant schemes (centrality Liang et al. (2025) , square clustering coefficients Ji et al. (2025b) , triangle count Southern et al. (2023) , etc.) where they apply. t = 1 t=1 t = 2 t=2 t = 3 t=3 Graph 1 Graph 2 0th Homology (Components) 1st Homology (Cycles) ( 1 , ∞ ) , ( 2 , 3 ) (1,\infty),(2,3) ( 2 , 2 ) , ( 2 , 2 ) , ( 2 , 2 ) , ( 3.3 ) (2,2),(2,2),(2,2),(3.3) ( 1 , − ) (1,-) None ( 1 , − ) , ( 2 , − ) (1,-),(2,-) ( 2 , 2 ) , ( 2 , 2 ) , ( 2 , 2 ) (2,2),(2,2),(2,2) None ( 3 , ∞ ) (3,\infty) Figure 1: Two non-isomorphic graphs with identical degree-based persistence. Vertex color encodes degree; edges inherit the color of their max-degree endpoint. Even under this canonical choice, a PD is far from a complete descriptor. Figure 1 shows two non-isomorphic graphs with identical degree-based PDs; in general, graphs with differing structures and connectivity patterns, can share the same PD under a given filtration scheme. Each PD therefore identifies a class of compatible graphs , and conditioning on a PD amounts to sampling from this class. This raises the natural question: given an input PD and filtration scheme Φ \Phi , can we generate strictly PD-compatible graphs under Φ \Phi ? This motivates a precise criterion for any PD-conditioned generator. Given a filtration scheme Φ \Phi and a graph G G , we let 𝒫 ⁡ ( G ∙ Φ ) \mathcal{P}(G^{\Phi}_{\bullet}) denote the PDs associated to the induced subgraph sequence of G G under Φ \Phi . We call a generator strictly PD-compliant if it satisfies 1. Soundness. Every sample G G from the generator satisfies 𝒫 ⁡ ( G ∙ Φ ) = D \mathcal{P}(G^{\Phi}_{\bullet})=D exactly. 2. Completeness. Every PD-compatible graph can be created by the generator. Soft-conditioned models violate soundness by construction. Aiming for strict PD-compliance is the natural starting point: it makes the conditioning problem precise, and exposes what an input PD does and does not pin down. Once strict compliance is attained, it can be relaxed in applications. Why exact compliance? Exact generation produces families of graphs with identical persistence diagrams but different combinatorial properties. Such families provide controlled datasets and benchmarks for training and evaluation in topological learning, and one can test whether a model truly exploits the prescribed topology or leans on unrelated statistics. They also give clean training and evaluation data for graph generation and reasoning from topological descriptors, with no label noise from approximate PD matching. Exact generation can also help find counterexamples to conjectures about what properties are determined by persistence, and approximate generation cannot serve this purpose at all. Affiliation: Aalto University Email: indradyumna.roy@aalto.fi Vikas Garg Affiliation: YaiYai Ltd & \& Aalto University Email: vgarg@csail.mit.edu Abstract Persistent homology summarizes the topological evolution of a graph as persistence diagrams (PDs). Generating graphs whose topology matches a target descriptor is increasingly important, yet existing topology-aware generative models rely on soft regularization, producing graphs whose PDs may only be approximately similar. We initiate a principled investigation of the generation problem: produce graphs that realize a target PD exactly. We propose two approaches guided by the implicit local and global constraints a target PD imposes. The local approach builds degree-based PD-equivalent graphs iteratively, and we prove that every output realizes the target PD and that every degree-based PD-equivalent graph is reachable. However, as shown thereafter, local generation necessarily trades off between sample diversity and reaching infeasible states. We therefore recast generation as a global constraint satisfaction problem with a complete encoding solvable by modern constraint programming solvers. This is applicable to any vertex-based permutation equivariant filtration scheme and is minimal under the degree filtration. Experiments on four standard graph generation benchmarks confirm that both methods realize the target PD exactly. Together, our methods provide a principled treatment of strict topology-compliant graph generation. Code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/ExactCompliance . 1 Introduction Topological structure is a primary driver of function in many real-world graphs. The presence of components, cycles, and higher-order voids govern stability and catalytic activity in molecules Xia et al. (2015) ; Townsend et al. (2020) ; Wang et al. (2025) , binding affinity and virality Wang et al. (2021) ; Wei (2022) , information flow in brain networks Sizemore et al. (2018) , certain patterns in medical imaging ( Meng et al., 2026 ) , and structural risk in transportation, trade, and infrastructure networks Woldemariam and Attoh-Okine (2025) ; Li et al. (2021) ; Villines (2026) . Persistent homology Carlsson (2009) ; Edelsbrunner and Morozov (2012) is the standard tool for extracting this information. Given a graph G G and a filtration scheme, persistent homology tracks the births and deaths of homological features along the induced subgraph sequence. The result is a multiset of pairs ( b , d ) (b,d) called the persistence diagram (PD). PDs are stable under perturbation ( Cohen-Steiner et al., 2006 ) , computable with efficient algorithms ( Otter et al., 2017 ) , and have become the workhorse of topological data analysis (TDA) in machine learning, underpinning almost every topology-aware approach to graph and higher-order neural networks ( Hofer et al., 2020 ; Immonen et al., 2023 ; Ballester and Rieck, 2025 ; Horn et al., 2021 ; Ji et al., 2025a ; Ji et al., 2026 ; Yan et al., 2022 ; Carriere et al., 2020 ; Russold and Kerber, 2024 ; Verma et al., 2024 ; Papamarkou et al., 2024 ) and providing topological signals that standard message passing alone cannot recover (e.g., cycle detection). In parallel, graph generation has recently emerged as a central tool across these same domains, with autoregressive ( You et al., 2018 ) , one-shot ( Simonovsky and Komodakis, 2018 ) , and diffusion-based ( Niu et al., 2020 ; Jo et al., 2022 ; Vignac et al., 2022 ) models. Recent work conditions generation on domain-specific structural properties: spectral profile ( Martinkus et al., 2022 ) , molecular validity ( De Cao and Kipf, 2018 ; Jin et al., 2020 ) , and structural constraints like planarity and acyclicity ( Madeira et al., 2024 ) . Conditioning on topology is a natural next step, but largely unexplored. A recent attempt Park et al. (2025) , augments discrete diffusion with a 1 1 -Wasserstein PD-matching loss. This soft regularizer nudges the learned distribution toward topological plausibility, but offers no guarantees that individually generated graphs attain the desired topological structure (e.g., the target number of cycles and components). items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.18853 (cs) [Submitted on 13 Oct 2026] Title: Two Clocks: Why Larger Rollout Batches Learn Slower but Fail on Schedule in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards Authors: Yuante Li , Junwei Quan , Kai Qiu , Kate Zhang , Yicheng Tao View a PDF of the paper titled Two Clocks: Why Larger Rollout Batches Learn Slower but Fail on Schedule in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards, by Yuante Li and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) relies on costly model-generated responses, motivating larger rollout batches and square-root learning-rate scaling. Reported to approximately preserve progress per sample with one optimizer step per rollout, this rule is less understood in practical multi-step training. We develop a two-clock framework that separates the samples needed to make progress from those consumed before collapse. Under a local quadratic model, the square-root rule preserves first-order drift per sample but not progress: larger batches take fewer, longer updates and lose more to curvature, yielding a learning-rate-dependent critical batch beyond which sample efficiency degrades. A drift-threshold hypothesis predicts a complementary failure clock whose sample count remains approximately invariant along the square-root rule. Controlled GRPO experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B across a $16\times$ batch range support both predictions. Ratio clipping delays failure, especially for larger batches, but the progress gap persists without it. Widening the clip trades stability for a transient speed gain. The progress gap reappears on another dataset, a general-purpose checkpoint, and a 7B model. Finally, we use the two-clock framework to derive a simple multi-step RLVR schedule: start below the critical batch and switch to a larger batch before failure. Our code is available at: this https URL . Two Clocks: Why Larger Rollout Batches Learn Slower but Fail on Schedule in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards Yuante Li † † thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Junwei Quan 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: University of Toronto yuantel@cs.cmu.edu, junwei.quan@mail.utoronto.ca Kai Qiu Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Kate Zhang Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Yicheng Tao Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Abstract Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) relies on costly model-generated responses, motivating larger rollout batches and square-root learning-rate scaling. Reported to approximately preserve progress per sample with one optimizer step per rollout, this rule is less understood in practical multi-step training. We develop a two-clock framework that separates the samples needed to make progress from those consumed before collapse. Under a local quadratic model, the square-root rule preserves first-order drift per sample but not progress: larger batches take fewer, longer updates and lose more to curvature, yielding a learning-rate-dependent critical batch beyond which sample efficiency degrades. A drift-threshold hypothesis predicts a complementary failure clock whose sample count remains approximately invariant along the square-root rule. Controlled GRPO experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B across a 16 × 16	imes batch range support both predictions. Ratio clipping delays failure, especially for larger batches, but the progress gap persists without it. Widening the clip trades stability for a transient speed gain. The progress gap reappears on another dataset, a general-purpose checkpoint, and a 7B model. Finally, we use the two-clock framework to derive a simple multi-step RLVR schedule: start below the critical batch and switch to a larger batch before failure. Our code is available at: two-clocks-rlvr . 1 Introduction Figure 1: The two clocks under the square-root rule with μ = 8 \mu{=}8 . Color marks the rollout batch, from 512 in blue to 8,192 in dark red. Left, with the clip: samples to reach 15% and 20% accuracy, with the critical-batch curve (gray) between perfect invariance (dotted) and the step-limited extreme (dashed). Right: samples to failure without the clip, against the failure-law band (gray), with an open marker for the run that never failed. Progress slows with the batch, while failure stays on the failure law. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) ( Lambert et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) has become a widely used post-training approach for language models, spanning mathematical reasoning ( Hubert et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2025 ) , code ( Wei et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025a ) , and broader domains scored against reference answers ( Su et al., 2025 ) . Its appeal is that large amounts of policy-generated data can be scored without human preference labels, but training remains expensive because this data must be regenerated as the policy changes: every policy update requires fresh rollouts, and generation dominates the cost. Practitioners therefore enlarge the rollout batch , the number of responses generated by one policy before it is updated, and rely on the square-root rule to transfer the learning rate across batch sizes, scaling it with the square root of the batch ( Malladi et al., 2022 ; Hilton et al., 2022 ) . For Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) with one optimizer step per rollout, the rule approximately works: rollout batches from 512 to 8K responses follow learning curves within about one accuracy point of each other when plotted against the number of samples consumed ( Li et al., 2026 ) . However, practical RLVR training rarely operates in this one-step regime. To amortize generation, practical RLVR recipes split each rollout into mini-batches and take one optimizer step on each. DAPO, for example, uses 16 optimizer steps per rollout ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . From the second step onward, the current policy has moved away from the policy that generated the data, so the token-level importance ratios depart from one and the PPO-style ratio clip begins to suppress gradient contributions from tokens whose ratios move beyond the clipping range. In our multi-step GRPO experiments, three phenomena appear together under the square-root rule: ➀ Progress slows with batch size. Larger rollout batches learn more slowly per sample. ➁ Failure keeps time in samples. Without the clip, larger batches collapse after the same number of samples as smaller ones, despite taking far fewer optimizer steps. ➂ Clipping helps larger batches most. Although clipping is often viewed as a bottleneck on learning ( Qi et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ) , its stabilizing effect is strongest for the larger batches. Figure 1 visualizes this split into two clocks: progress becomes increasingly sample-inefficient with larger rollout batches, while failure stays locked to the number of samples consumed. Prior work studies these effects separately: batch-size invariance ( Hilton et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , critical-batch behavior with the learning rate tuned at every batch ( McCandlish et al., 2018 ) , and clipping at a fixed batch size. None explains why all three emerge together under the same batch-dependent learning-rate rule. We explain these phenomena with a two-clock framework of batch scaling. Its central observation is that the square-root rule preserves the policy’s drift per sample, the persistent displacement it accumulates, but not the progress that drift produces. A larger rollout batch takes fewer optimizer steps on the same samples, and the square-root rule makes each step longer. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.18839 (cs) [Submitted on 13 Oct 2026] Title: Fast Rates for Offline Q-Learning with KL Regularization Authors: Yize Hao , Guangxin Jiang , Shuang Qiu View a PDF of the paper titled Fast Rates for Offline Q-Learning with KL Regularization, by Yize Hao and Guangxin Jiang and Shuang Qiu View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: This paper investigates offline Q-learning for finite-horizon Markov decision processes with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. Recent studies have shown that KL regularization can yield fast rates in offline decision-making problems. However, it remains unclear whether Q-learning, which adopts incremental stochastic approximation updates, can achieve such fast rates in the offline setting. We first propose KL-regularized Q-Learning (KLQ), a simple variant of classical Q-learning. By exploiting KL regularization, we prove that KLQ achieves a sample complexity of $\widetilde{O}(1/\epsilon)$ without explicit pessimism. This guarantee, however, has an exponential dependence on the KL regularization parameter and the horizon. To address this limitation, we further propose KL-regularized Pessimistic Q-Learning (KLPQ), which incorporates pessimism into KLQ. We prove that KLPQ retains the same \(\widetilde O(1/\epsilon)\) rate while removing the explicit exponential dependence, thereby further improving the sample complexity. To the best of our knowledge, these results establish the first fast-rate guarantees for offline Q-learning in tabular finite-horizon KL-regularized MDPs. items.content: Fast Rates for Offline Q-Learning with KL Regularization Yize Hao Guangxin Jiang Shuang Qiu † October 13, 2026 Abstract This paper investigates offline Q-learning for finite-horizon Markov decision processes with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. Recent studies have shown that KL regularization can yield fast rates in offline decision-making problems. However, it remains unclear whether Q-learning, which adopts incremental stochastic approximation updates, can achieve such fast rates in the offline setting. We first propose KL-regularized Q-Learning (KLQ), a simple variant of classical Q-learning. By exploiting KL regularization, we prove that KLQ achieves a sample complexity of O ~ ​ ( 1 / ϵ ) \widetilde{O}(1/\epsilon) without explicit pessimism. This guarantee, however, has an exponential dependence on the KL regularization parameter and the horizon. To address this limitation, we further propose KL-regularized Pessimistic Q-Learning (KLPQ), which incorporates pessimism into KLQ. We prove that KLPQ retains the same O ~ ​ ( 1 / ϵ ) \widetilde{O}(1/\epsilon) rate while removing the explicit exponential dependence, thereby further improving the sample complexity. To the best of our knowledge, these results establish the first fast-rate guarantees for offline Q-learning in tabular finite-horizon KL-regularized MDPs. 0 0 footnotetext: Corresponding Author 1 1 footnotetext: Harbin Institute of Technology. Email: 24b910001@stu.hit.edu.cn 2 2 footnotetext: City University of Hong Kong. Email: yizehao3-c@my.cityu.edu.hk 3 3 footnotetext: Harbin Institute of Technology. Email: gxjiang@hit.edu.cn 4 4 footnotetext: City University of Hong Kong. Email: shuanqiu@cityu.edu.hk 1 Introduction Offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn a near-optimal policy from a fixed dataset without further interaction with the environment ( Levine et al., 2020 ) . A central challenge in this setting is limited data coverage: since the learner cannot collect additional samples, the learned policy may select actions that are poorly represented in the offline data, leading to inaccurate value estimates and extrapolation error ( Fujimoto et al., 2019 ; Kumar et al., 2020 ) . Two prominent approaches used to stabilize offline learning are pessimism and policy regularization. Pessimistic methods penalize value estimates in poorly covered regions to mitigate estimation errors caused by insufficient data ( Rashidinejad et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2021 ; Shi et al., 2022 ) . Policy regularization instead constrains the learned policy relative to a reference policy, with the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence being a widely used choice. When the reference policy coincides with the behavior policy that generates the offline data, KL regularization serves as behavior regularization, keeping the learned policy close to the behavior policy and thereby reducing distribution shift and extrapolation error ( Wu et al., 2019 ) . The reference policy, however, may differ from the behavior policy. In this case, KL regularization no longer directly constrains the learned policy toward the behavior policy. Nevertheless, Chen et al. (2026) show that KL regularization with respect to a fixed reference policy can stabilize offline learning in Markov games under unilateral concentrability. The practical importance of regularization is also reflected in reinforcement learning from human feedback and preference-based learning, where KL regularization is widely used to keep the learned policy close to a reference model ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Xiong et al., 2023 ; Rafailov et al., 2023 ) . These developments motivate a deeper understanding of the statistical role of KL regularization in offline learning. Recent theoretical work has revealed that KL regularization can substantially change the statistical behavior of offline learning. In single-step decision problems, fast rates have been established for KL-regularized contextual and multi-armed bandits ( Zhao et al., 2025a ; Zhao et al., 2026b ; Ji et al., 2026a ) . Related results have also been established under forward-KL regularization ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) . With KL regularization, these works achieve a sample complexity of O ~ ​ ( 1 / ϵ ) \widetilde{O}(1/\epsilon) , in contrast to the O ~ ​ ( 1 / ϵ 2 ) \widetilde{O}(1/\epsilon^{2}) sample complexity typically obtained in standard unregularized settings. Fast rates have also been established for single-step zero-sum games ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) and general-sum games ( Chen and Zhang, 2026b ) . More recently, these results have been extended to multi-step sequential decision problems. In particular, Chen et al. (2026) establish a sample complexity of O ~ ​ ( 1 / ϵ ) \widetilde{O}(1/\epsilon) for offline two-player zero-sum Markov games with KL regularization. From an algorithmic perspective, the methods of Chen et al. (2026) can be regarded as fitted Q-iteration. Their approach proceeds via backward induction, where Q-functions are estimated stagewise from the end of the horizon to the beginning. In contrast, another important class of algorithms is Q-learning, which adopts incremental stochastic approximation updates to solve the Bellman optimality equation ( Watkins and Dayan, 1992 ) . Understanding the statistical efficiency and convergence behavior of Q-learning remains an important topic in the theory of reinforcement learning ( Li et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . The resulting update scheme differs fundamentally from backward induction, and existing fast-rate analyses based on backward induction do not establish analogous guarantees for Q-learning. In the offline RL setting, Shi et al. (2022) established finite-sample guarantees for pessimistic Q-learning under the standard unregularized objective and single-policy concentrability. Nevertheless, whether offline Q-learning can achieve fast rates for the KL-regularized objective remains unclear. This leads to the following question: Can offline Q-learning achieve fast rates with KL regularization? The above question poses three main challenges. First, although fast rates have been established for KL-regularized offline learning in several settings, the incremental updates of Q-learning pose additional challenges for finite-sample analysis, making it unclear how to exploit KL regularization to achieve similar fast rates. Second, existing finite-sample guarantees for offline Q-learning are established for the unregularized objective and rely on the principle of pessimism. It remains unclear whether pessimism is still necessary with KL regularization, or whether KL regularization alone can enable Q-learning to achieve fast rates. Third, the impact of pessimism on sample complexity under KL regularization remains underexplored for offline Q-learning. In this paper, we address these challenges and therefore answer this question affirmatively by developing two offline Q-learning algorithms for tabular finite-horizon KL-regularized MDPs. For an MDP with S S states and A A actions, let η > 0 \eta>0 denote the KL regularization parameter and let C η ⋆ C_{\eta}^{\star} denote the single-policy concentrability coefficient for the corresponding KL-regularized optimal policy. Given K K offline trajectories of horizon H H , our main contributions are summarized as follows. • We first introduce KL-regularized Q-Learning (KLQ), a simple variant of classical Q-learning without the principle of pessimism. We prove that KLQ achieves a sample complexity of O ~ ​ ( η ​ e η ​ H ​ ( H + 1 ) ​ H 8 ​ S ​ A ​ C η ⋆ / ϵ ) \widetilde{O}\!\left(\eta e^{\eta H(H+1)}H^{8}SAC^{\star}_{\eta}/\epsilon\right) for finding an ϵ \epsilon -optimal policy. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first O ~ ​ ( 1 / ϵ ) \widetilde{O}(1/\epsilon) sample complexity guarantee for Q-learning in an offline finite-horizon tabular setting. This result also demonstrates that pessimism is not necessary for achieving fast rates. • Based on KLQ, we propose KL-regularized Pessimistic Q-Learning (KLPQ), which further incorporates pessimism into KL-regularized Q-Learning. We prove that KLPQ achieves an improved sample complexity of O ~ ​ ( η ​ H 7 ​ S ​ A ​ C η ⋆ / ϵ ) \widetilde{O}\left(\eta H^{7}SAC_{\eta}^{\star}/\epsilon\right) . This removes KLQ’s explicit exponential dependence on the regularization parameter and horizon while retaining the fast rate. • On the technical side, we exploit the structure induced by KL regularization to establish a fast rate analysis of incremental Q-learning updates through a recursion for the squared Q-estimation error. We further show that pessimism sharpens both this error recursion and the conversion from Q-estimation error to policy suboptimality. 1.1 Related Work Offline RL. A large body of theoretical work studies offline RL under coverage conditions, with pessimism playing an important role in controlling estimation errors caused by insufficient data coverage ( Rashidinejad et al., 2021 ; Xie et al., 2021b ; Jin et al., 2021 ; Shi et al., 2022 ; Xie et al., 2021a ; Yan et al., 2023 ; Qiao et al., 2026 ) . This principle has been developed for both model-based and model-free methods ( Rashidinejad et al., 2021 ; Xie et al., 2021b ; Uehara and Sun, 2021 ; Shi et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) . Beyond the tabular setting, finite-sample guarantees have also been established with function approximation under partial coverage assumptions ( Zhan et al., 2022 ; Xiong et al., 2022 ; Ye et al., 2023 ; Uehara et al., 2023 ) . Fast Rates in KL-Regularized Learning. KL regularization can fundamentally change the statistical behavior of learning problems. In the online setting, for single-step problems, fast rates have been established for KL-regularized contextual bandits and RLHF ( Zhao et al., 2025a ) , while logarithmic regret has also been established for KL-regularized multi-armed bandits ( Ji et al., 2026b ) . For multi-step tabular problems, fast rates have been established for maximum entropy exploration ( Tiapkin et al., 2023 ) and sequential RL with demonstration regularization ( Tiapkin et al., 2024 ) . In particular, the entropy regularization considered by Tiapkin et al. (2023) is equivalent to KL regularization with a uniform reference policy, up to an additive constant. Zhao et al. (2025b) establish logarithmic regret for KL-regularized episodic RL, while logarithmic regret has also been established for KL-regularized zero-sum Markov games ( Nayak et al., 2025 ) . Beyond the tabular setting, Hong et al. (2026) study KL-regularized RL with function approximation under misspecification. In offline learning, for single-step problems, fast rates are known for KL-regularized contextual and multi-armed bandits ( Zhao et al., 2026b ; Ji et al., 2026a ; Zhao et al., 2026a ) , as well as preference learning and games ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Chen and Zhang, 2026b ) . The role of pessimism has also been studied in this setting. Ji et al. (2026a) establish matching upper and lower bounds across different regularization regimes for offline KL-regularized multi-armed bandits. Their algorithm constructs a pessimistic reward estimate and achieves the optimal sample complexity in both regimes. In contrast, Wu et al. (2025) , Zhang et al. (2026) , and Chen and Zhang (2026b) obtain fast rates without explicit pessimistic estimates in their respective settings. For multi-step decision problems, Chen et al. (2026) establish a sample complexity of O ~ ​ ( 1 / ϵ ) \widetilde{O}(1/\epsilon) for offline Markov games with KL regularization. Their theoretical construction uses backward induction and is therefore different from the incremental Q-learning updates considered in this work. Q-Learning. Q-learning is a classical model-free method for solving the Bellman optimality equation ( Watkins and Dayan, 1992 ; Even-Dar and Mansour, 2003 ) . Under the standard unregularized objective, its non-asymptotic theory has been developed in several settings. For finite-horizon episodic MDPs, regret guarantees have been established for online Q-learning ( Jin et al., 2018 ; Li et al., 2021b ) , while finite-sample guarantees have also been established for offline Q-learning under single-policy concentrability ( Shi et al., 2022 ) . For discounted MDPs, Q-learning has been studied under a generative model ( Li et al., 2021a ; Li et al., 2024 ) , with Markovian samples ( Qu and Wierman, 2020 ; Li et al., 2020 ) , and in the offline setting under partial coverage ( Yan et al., 2023 ) . These results typically exhibit an O ~ ​ ( ϵ − 2 ) \widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) dependence on accuracy for Q-function estimation or policy suboptimality. With linear function approximation, Liu et al. (2025) establish L 2 L^{2} convergence rates of Q-learning to a bounded set. Finite-sample analyses have also been developed for average-reward Q-learning, under span contraction conditions ( Zhang et al., 2021 ) and, more recently, for weakly communicating MDPs ( Jiao et al., 2026 ) . For regularized objectives, Uehara et al. (2023) study offline learning under partial coverage using soft Q-functions, but estimate the Q-functions through minimax optimization. Jeong and Lee (2024) ; Jeong and Lee (2025) provide finite-time analyses of soft Q-learning in discounted tabular MDPs under full state-action coverage, while Xi et al. The resulting update scheme differs fundamentally from backward induction, and existing fast-rate analyses based on backward induction do not establish analogous guarantees for Q-learning. In the offline RL setting, Shi et al. (2022) established finite-sample guarantees for pessimistic Q-learning under the standard unregularized objective and single-policy concentrability. Nevertheless, whether offline Q-learning can achieve fast rates for the KL-regularized objective remains unclear. This leads to the following question: Can offline Q-learning achieve fast rates with KL regularization? The above question poses three main challenges. First, although fast rates have been established for KL-regularized offline learning in several settings, the incremental updates of Q-learning pose additional challenges for finite-sample analysis, making it unclear how to exploit KL regularization to achieve similar fast rates. Second, existing finite-sample guarantees for offline Q-learning are established for the unregularized objective and rely on the principle of pessimism. It remains unclear whether pessimism is still necessary with KL regularization, or whether KL regularization alone can enable Q-learning to achieve fast rates. Third, the impact of pessimism on sample complexity under KL regularization remains underexplored for offline Q-learning. In this paper, we address these challenges and therefore answer this question affirmatively by developing two offline Q-learning algorithms for tabular finite-horizon KL-regularized MDPs. For an MDP with S S states and A A actions, let η > 0 \eta>0 denote the KL regularization parameter and let C η ⋆ C_{\eta}^{\star} denote the single-policy concentrability coefficient for the corresponding KL-regularized optimal policy. Given K K offline trajectories of horizon H H , our main contributions are summarized as follows. • We first introduce KL-regularized Q-Learning (KLQ), a simple variant of classical Q-learning without the principle of pessimism. We prove that KLQ achieves a sample complexity of O ~ ​ ( η ​ e η ​ H ​ ( H + 1 ) ​ H 8 ​ S ​ A ​ C η ⋆ / ϵ ) \widetilde{O}\!\left(\eta e^{\eta H(H+1)}H^{8}SAC^{\star}_{\eta}/\epsilon\right) for finding an ϵ \epsilon -optimal policy. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first O ~ ​ ( 1 / ϵ ) \widetilde{O}(1/\epsilon) sample complexity guarantee for Q-learning in an offline finite-horizon tabular setting. This result also demonstrates that pessimism is not necessary for achieving fast rates. • Based on KLQ, we propose KL-regularized Pessimistic Q-Learning (KLPQ), which further incorporates pessimism into KL-regularized Q-Learning. We prove that KLPQ achieves an improved sample complexity of O ~ ​ ( η ​ H 7 ​ S ​ A ​ C η ⋆ / ϵ ) \widetilde{O}\left(\eta H^{7}SAC_{\eta}^{\star}/\epsilon\right) . This removes KLQ’s explicit exponential dependence on the regularization parameter and horizon while retaining the fast rate. • On the technical side, we exploit the structure induced by KL regularization to establish a fast rate analysis of incremental Q-learning updates through a recursion for the squared Q-estimation error. We further show that pessimism sharpens both this error recursion and the conversion from Q-estimation error to policy suboptimality. 1.1 Related Work Offline RL. A large body of theoretical work studies offline RL under coverage conditions, with pessimism playing an important role in controlling estimation errors caused by insufficient data coverage ( Rashidinejad et al., 2021 ; Xie et al., 2021b ; Jin et al., 2021 ; Shi et al., 2022 ; Xie et al., 2021a ; Yan et al., 2023 ; Qiao et al., 2026 ) . This principle has been developed for both model-based and model-free methods ( Rashidinejad et al., 2021 ; Xie et al., 2021b ; Uehara and Sun, 2021 ; Shi et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) . Beyond the tabular setting, finite-sample guarantees have also been established with function approximation under partial coverage assumptions ( Zhan et al., 2022 ; Xiong et al., 2022 ; Ye et al., 2023 ; Uehara et al., 2023 ) . Fast Rates in KL-Regularized Learning. KL regularization can fundamentally change the statistical behavior of learning problems. In the online setting, for single-step problems, fast rates have been established for KL-regularized contextual bandits and RLHF ( Zhao et al., 2025a ) , while logarithmic regret has also been established for KL-regularized multi-armed bandits ( Ji et al., 2026b ) . For multi-step tabular problems, fast rates have been established for maximum entropy exploration ( Tiapkin et al., 2023 ) and sequential RL with demonstration regularization ( Tiapkin et al., 2024 ) . In particular, the entropy regularization considered by Tiapkin et al. (2023) is equivalent to KL regularization with a uniform reference policy, up to an additive constant. Zhao et al. (2025b) establish logarithmic regret for KL-regularized episodic RL, while logarithmic regret has also been established for KL-regularized zero-sum Markov games ( Nayak et al., 2025 ) . Beyond the tabular setting, Hong et al. (2026) study KL-regularized RL with function approximation under misspecification. In offline learning, for single-step problems, fast rates are known for KL-regularized contextual and multi-armed bandits ( Zhao et al., 2026b ; Ji et al., 2026a ; Zhao et al., 2026a ) , as well as preference learning and games ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Chen and Zhang, 2026b ) . The role of pessimism has also been studied in this setting. Ji et al. (2026a) establish matching upper and lower bounds across different regularization regimes for offline KL-regularized multi-armed bandits. Their algorithm constructs a pessimistic reward estimate and achieves the optimal sample complexity in both regimes. In contrast, Wu et al. (2025) , Zhang et al. (2026) , and Chen and Zhang (2026b) obtain fast rates without explicit pessimistic estimates in their respective settings. For multi-step decision problems, Chen et al. (2026) establish a sample complexity of O ~ ​ ( 1 / ϵ ) \widetilde{O}(1/\epsilon) for offline Markov games with KL regularization. Their theoretical construction uses backward induction and is therefore different from the incremental Q-learning updates considered in this work. Q-Learning. Q-learning is a classical model-free method for solving the Bellman optimality equation ( Watkins and Dayan, 1992 ; Even-Dar and Mansour, 2003 ) . Under the standard unregularized objective, its non-asymptotic theory has been developed in several settings. For finite-horizon episodic MDPs, regret guarantees have been established for online Q-learning ( Jin et al., 2018 ; Li et al., 2021b ) , while finite-sample guarantees have also been established for offline Q-learning under single-policy concentrability ( Shi et al., 2022 ) . For discounted MDPs, Q-learning has been studied under a generative model ( Li et al., 2021a ; Li et al., 2024 ) , with Markovian samples ( Qu and Wierman, 2020 ; Li et al., 2020 ) , and in the offline setting under partial coverage ( Yan et al., 2023 ) . These results typically exhibit an O ~ ​ ( ϵ − 2 ) \widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) dependence on accuracy for Q-function estimation or policy suboptimality. With linear function approximation, Liu et al. (2025) establish L 2 L^{2} convergence rates of Q-learning to a bounded set. Finite-sample analyses have also been developed for average-reward Q-learning, under span contraction conditions ( Zhang et al., 2021 ) and, more recently, for weakly communicating MDPs ( Jiao et al., 2026 ) . For regularized objectives, Uehara et al. (2023) study offline learning under partial coverage using soft Q-functions, but estimate the Q-functions through minimax optimization. Jeong and Lee (2024) ; Jeong and Lee (2025) provide finite-time analyses of soft Q-learning in discounted tabular MDPs under full state-action coverage, while Xi et al. (2025) study regularized Q-learning with linear function approximation using an algorithm with two time scales. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.18860 (cs) [Submitted on 13 Oct 2026] Title: AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards Authors: Xin Gao , Yifan Yang , Xin Li , Pan Wang , Yan Li , Muzhao Tian , Mingxi Cheng , Bei Liu , Kai Qiu , Qi Dai , Dong Chen , Yue Dong , Leandros Tassiulas , Rex Ying , Ji Li , Chong Luo View a PDF of the paper titled AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards, by Xin Gao and 15 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Generating information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards as code is appealing because the outputs are structured, editable, and verifiable. Yet code models cannot see how their choices of layout and color come together on the canvas, often limiting spatial planning and aesthetic quality. Image generators excel at visual design but can misrender requested content, making their outputs unreliable targets for direct reproduction. We therefore introduce AesCode, which generates code grounded in the content prompt while using an image generated from the same prompt as an aesthetic guidance. To do so, AesCode represents the target as a design graph that describes the whole canvas and makes each property attributable. From this graph, we derive complementary cross-modal rewards: deterministic verifiers score properties parsable from code and rendering, while a VLM judge assesses the non-parsable ones with a sample-specific Visual Graph Rubric (VGR) tied to graph elements and relations. We optimize these decoupled rewards through reinforcement learning with per-channel normalization to jointly improve spatial planning, aesthetic quality, and verifiable correctness. To evaluate this setting, we build a benchmark that scores verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with visual scores highly consistent with human judgments. We find that reference images substantially improve the visual quality of code generated by existing models, and ablations show that AesCode benefits from references both as model input and as a source of visual rewards. Relative to same-scale Qwen3-VL baselines given the same references, AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B improve visual quality by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points, reaching scores comparable to those of closed-source frontier models such as GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8. Oct 2026 AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards Xin Gao 2,∗ Yifan Yang 1,† Xin Li 3 Pan Wang 4 Yan Li 5 Muzhao Tian 6 Mingxi Cheng 1 Bei Liu 1 Kai Qiu 1 Qi Dai 1 Dong Chen 1 Yue Dong 1 Leandros Tassiulas 2,† Rex Ying 2,† Ji Li 1 Chong Luo 1 1 Microsoft 2 Yale University 3 Nanyang Technological University 4 University of Pittsburgh 5 Shanghai Jiao Tong University 6 Fudan University Generating information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards as code is appealing because the outputs are structured, editable, and verifiable. Yet code models cannot see how their choices of layout and color come together on the canvas, often limiting spatial planning and aesthetic quality. Image generators excel at visual design but can misrender requested content, making their outputs unreliable targets for direct reproduction. We therefore introduce AesCode, which generates code grounded in the content prompt while using an image generated from the same prompt as an aesthetic guidance. To do so, AesCode represents the target as a design graph that describes the whole canvas and makes each property attributable. From this graph, we derive complementary cross-modal rewards: deterministic verifiers score properties parsable from code and rendering, while a VLM judge assesses the non-parsable ones with a sample-specific Visual Graph Rubric (VGR) tied to graph elements and relations. We optimize these decoupled rewards through reinforcement learning with per-channel normalization to jointly improve spatial planning, aesthetic quality, and verifiable correctness. To evaluate this setting, we build a benchmark that scores verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with visual scores highly consistent with human judgments. We find that reference images substantially improve the visual quality of code generated by existing models, and ablations show that AesCode benefits from references both as model input and as a source of visual rewards. Relative to same-scale Qwen3-VL baselines given the same references, AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B improve visual quality by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points, reaching scores comparable to those of closed-source frontier models such as GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8. Project Page: https://microsoft.github.io/AesCode/ Correspondence: yifanyang@microsoft.com , { leandros.tassiulas , rex.ying } @yale.edu † Corresponding authors. ∗ Work was done during an internship at Microsoft Research Asia. Figure 1 : Information-rich infographics generated as code. Prompts specify content, while image-generator references offer visual design guidance. The examples show a landscape dashboard and portrait poster rendered from generated HTML/CSS. Introduction Information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards pack dense content into a single canvas [ 29 , 45 ] . Generating them as code is highly desirable because the output remains structured, editable, and verifiable. However, code models suffer from a fundamental limitation: they cannot “see” the canvas. Spatial layout, hierarchy, and color are declared line by line, resulting in outputs that satisfy content constraints but often appear visually dated. In contrast, image generators excel at composing visually striking pages [ 8 , 10 ] , yet frequently misrender text, numbers, and logical relations, producing raster outputs that cannot be edited or verified [ 23 , 37 ] . These complementary strengths motivate a novel setting where an image generator provides an aesthetic guidance for the code model. Specifically, a reference image generated from the same prompt serves as a conditional input to supply layout and style inspiration. While existing image-to-code methods [ 1 , 36 , 14 ] also use images as input, they treat them as absolute ground truth for pixel-level reconstruction. This rigid replication and its associated image-level metrics [ 6 , 42 , 21 ] fail in our setting because they force the code model to mimic the hallucinated content of the generated prior and penalize valid design variations. Our fundamental setting therefore challenges the code model to strictly satisfy the prompt’s content while flexibly extracting layout and style from a noisy reference image. Simply providing the reference image as an input is insufficient. Off-the-shelf vision-language models (VLMs) naturally entangle visual features with text semantics. When given a noisy reference, they tend to either reproduce its hallucinated content or ignore its layout entirely. The model therefore requires explicit training to extract the aesthetic prior while adhering to the text prompt. To facilitate this, we propose AesCode, which conceptualizes the generated target as a Design Graph. This structured intermediate representation explicitly separates semantic information from visual cues. Within this graph, nodes represent distinct functional elements such as text blocks, tables, and charts. Each node possesses decoupled attributes for its required content (e.g., specific strings or data series) and its visual properties (e.g., bounding boxes and colors). Edges explicitly define structural relationships, including hierarchical containment and spatial alignment. Because the graph structure makes individual properties explicitly attributable, it naturally enables decoupled reward channels tailored to distinct objectives. Blending mixed outcomes into a single score (e.g., rendering correct text but a chaotic layout) often misaligns training gradients. To preserve specific learning signals, we derive synergic cross-modal rewards directly from the graph: deterministic verifiers provide fast, absolute checks for properties readable from code and DOM rendering, while a VLM judge assesses aesthetics through a Visual Graph Rubric (VGR), avoiding unstable holistic scoring by answering node-specific binary questions. We then balance these channels using Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization (GDPO) [ 24 ] , preventing dense verification signals from overwhelming sparse aesthetic feedback. We also release an infographic benchmark evaluating verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with automated visual scores closely matching human judgments. Ablations confirm that reference images consistently improve visual quality as an aesthetic prior across all tested models. Given the same references, our AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B gain 31.1 and 22.4 Visual points over their Qwen3-VL backbones, achieving visual quality comparable to frontier models like GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 while making noticeably fewer content errors. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce a novel paradigm for aesthetic code generation that utilizes image generators as an aesthetic prior. A reference image generated from the same prompt conditions the code model as input and provides visual signals during training. • We propose AesCode, which introduces decoupled cross-modal rewards driven by a design graph. It pairs deterministic verifiers for structural correctness with a sample-specific, graph-based VLM judge for aesthetic quality. • We release an infographic benchmark that evaluates correctness and visual quality separately, with human-aligned visual scores. References help every model we test, and AesCode matches leading proprietary models visually while following the prompt more closely. Related Work Visual Design and Code Generation. Posters, slides, and infographics can be generated as images or code. Image generators such as PosterMaker [ 10 ] and BizGen [ 30 ] compose appealing pages, but still misrender text and data on dense content [ 37 ] , and their raster outputs cannot be edited. Code is editable and verifiable. When written from text alone, as in LIDA [ 7 ] and PPTAgent [ 45 ] , it is composed without seeing the page and often looks plain. When written from an image, as in Design2Code [ 36 ] and ChartMimic [ 41 ] , it copies the input as ground truth. Closest to ours, DesignAsCode [ 26 ] and Editable Visual Design [ 43 ] let a coding agent consult a generated image, but only at inference time; the code model is never trained to use it. We instead train the code model to follow a prompt-generated image as an aesthetic prior for layout and style. Reward Design for Visual Generation. RL training requires a reward for the rendered page. In image-to-code, this reward is usually similarity to the input image, measured with visual metrics [ 33 , 3 ] or MLLM critics [ 42 , 21 ] . For a generated reference, however, this would penalize valid alternatives and reward copied errors. Without a target image, rule-based rewards are precise but limited to what a program can check, such as element overlap in AeSlides [ 28 ] , while holistic MLLM judges [ 46 , 2 ] give scores that shift with prompt phrasing. A more stable alternative breaks one judgment into many yes/no questions, first for text-to-image evaluation [ 4 ] and more recently as rubric rewards for RL [ 12 , 31 ] . These questions, however, are derived from text alone and cannot check the design a reference proposes. We therefore build a design graph from the prompt and the reference, verify code-level properties with rules, and turn the remaining visual properties into a Visual Graph Rubric (VGR) tied to graph elements. Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning. Critic-free methods such as GRPO [ 35 ] normalize rewards within a sampled group and, following DeepSeek-R1 [ 13 ] , have become a standard recipe for post-training LLMs and VLMs [ 25 ] . They assume a single reward, however: when several rewards are summed before normalization, a dense, near-saturated rule reward can drown out a sparse aesthetic one. MO-GRPO [ 16 ] reweights rewards by their variance, while GDPO [ 24 ] normalizes each reward separately. We adopt GDPO to balance our rule-based and VGR rewards. Appendix A extends this review with a fuller discussion of each of the three threads above. Method AesCode learns visual design through graph-structured supervision. We first construct a target design graph that combines prompt-required content with non-authoritative reference cues ( Section 3.1 ). We then route its properties to deterministic and perceptual reward channels ( Section 3.2 ) and optimize them with SFT and GDPO [ 24 ] ( Section 3.3 ). Finally, we define a separate evaluation protocol for factual correctness and human-aligned visual quality ( Section 3.4 ). Design Graph as a Supervision Target The prompt p p specifies required information, while visual design admits many valid solutions. Learning needs a concrete signal, so an image generator supplies one compelling possibility I ref I_{\mathrm{ref}} , which may be factually or structurally wrong. We therefore organize supervision as a design graph rather than a monolithic target, scoring prompt-derived requirements independently of the reference. We define the supervision target as 𝒢 tgt = ( 𝒱 , ℰ , 𝐗 V , r ) = Φ ⁡ ( p , I ref ) , \mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{tgt}}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\mathbf{X}_{V},r)=\Phi(p,I_{\mathrm{ref}}), (1) where the canvas root r r holds page-level attributes and contains every top-level element. The remaining nodes come from a closed vocabulary of atomic elements, such as text, images, charts, tables, and badges, and of containers, such as regions, cards, panels, lists, and groups, which hold other nodes instead of rendering content; three or more interchangeable siblings collapse into one group node with a count attribute. Attributes 𝐗 V \mathbf{X}_{V} record content, geometry, and appearance, including structured chart and table data, and each edge ( u , τ , v ) ∈ ℰ (u,	au,v)\in\mathcal{E} carries a relation type τ 	au covering containment, alignment, order, adjacency, and semantic connection. This decomposition lets prompt requirements and reference cues constrain complementary properties independently, making supervision attributable across semantic dimensions, and since it assumes only elements and their two-dimensional structure, it applies broadly to structured visual artifacts. Oct 2026 AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards Xin Gao 2,∗ Yifan Yang 1,† Xin Li 3 Pan Wang 4 Yan Li 5 Muzhao Tian 6 Mingxi Cheng 1 Bei Liu 1 Kai Qiu 1 Qi Dai 1 Dong Chen 1 Yue Dong 1 Leandros Tassiulas 2,† Rex Ying 2,† Ji Li 1 Chong Luo 1 1 Microsoft 2 Yale University 3 Nanyang Technological University 4 University of Pittsburgh 5 Shanghai Jiao Tong University 6 Fudan University Generating information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards as code is appealing because the outputs are structured, editable, and verifiable. Yet code models cannot see how their choices of layout and color come together on the canvas, often limiting spatial planning and aesthetic quality. Image generators excel at visual design but can misrender requested content, making their outputs unreliable targets for direct reproduction. We therefore introduce AesCode, which generates code grounded in the content prompt while using an image generated from the same prompt as an aesthetic guidance. To do so, AesCode represents the target as a design graph that describes the whole canvas and makes each property attributable. From this graph, we derive complementary cross-modal rewards: deterministic verifiers score properties parsable from code and rendering, while a VLM judge assesses the non-parsable ones with a sample-specific Visual Graph Rubric (VGR) tied to graph elements and relations. We optimize these decoupled rewards through reinforcement learning with per-channel normalization to jointly improve spatial planning, aesthetic quality, and verifiable correctness. To evaluate this setting, we build a benchmark that scores verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with visual scores highly consistent with human judgments. We find that reference images substantially improve the visual quality of code generated by existing models, and ablations show that AesCode benefits from references both as model input and as a source of visual rewards. Relative to same-scale Qwen3-VL baselines given the same references, AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B improve visual quality by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points, reaching scores comparable to those of closed-source frontier models such as GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8. Figure 1 : Information-rich infographics generated as code. Prompts specify content, while image-generator references offer visual design guidance. The examples show a landscape dashboard and portrait poster rendered from generated HTML/CSS. Introduction Information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards pack dense content into a single canvas [ 29 , 45 ] . Generating them as code is highly desirable because the output remains structured, editable, and verifiable. However, code models suffer from a fundamental limitation: they cannot “see” the canvas. Spatial layout, hierarchy, and color are declared line by line, resulting in outputs that satisfy content constraints but often appear visually dated. In contrast, image generators excel at composing visually striking pages [ 8 , 10 ] , yet frequently misrender text, numbers, and logical relations, producing raster outputs that cannot be edited or verified [ 23 , 37 ] . These complementary strengths motivate a novel setting where an image generator provides an aesthetic guidance for the code model. Specifically, a reference image generated from the same prompt serves as a conditional input to supply layout and style inspiration. While existing image-to-code methods [ 1 , 36 , 14 ] also use images as input, they treat them as absolute ground truth for pixel-level reconstruction. This rigid replication and its associated image-level metrics [ 6 , 42 , 21 ] fail in our setting because they force the code model to mimic the hallucinated content of the generated prior and penalize valid design variations. Our fundamental setting therefore challenges the code model to strictly satisfy the prompt’s content while flexibly extracting layout and style from a noisy reference image. Simply providing the reference image as an input is insufficient. Off-the-shelf vision-language models (VLMs) naturally entangle visual features with text semantics. When given a noisy reference, they tend to either reproduce its hallucinated content or ignore its layout entirely. The model therefore requires explicit training to extract the aesthetic prior while adhering to the text prompt. To facilitate this, we propose AesCode, which conceptualizes the generated target as a Design Graph. This structured intermediate representation explicitly separates semantic information from visual cues. Within this graph, nodes represent distinct functional elements such as text blocks, tables, and charts. Each node possesses decoupled attributes for its required content (e.g., specific strings or data series) and its visual properties (e.g., bounding boxes and colors). Edges explicitly define structural relationships, including hierarchical containment and spatial alignment. Because the graph structure makes individual properties explicitly attributable, it naturally enables decoupled reward channels tailored to distinct objectives. Blending mixed outcomes into a single score (e.g., rendering correct text but a chaotic layout) often misaligns training gradients. To preserve specific learning signals, we derive synergic cross-modal rewards directly from the graph: deterministic verifiers provide fast, absolute checks for properties readable from code and DOM rendering, while a VLM judge assesses aesthetics through a Visual Graph Rubric (VGR), avoiding unstable holistic scoring by answering node-specific binary questions. We then balance these channels using Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization (GDPO) [ 24 ] , preventing dense verification signals from overwhelming sparse aesthetic feedback. We also release an infographic benchmark evaluating verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with automated visual scores closely matching human judgments. Ablations confirm that reference images consistently improve visual quality as an aesthetic prior across all tested models. Given the same references, our AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B gain 31.1 and 22.4 Visual points over their Qwen3-VL backbones, achieving visual quality comparable to frontier models like GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 while making noticeably fewer content errors. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce a novel paradigm for aesthetic code generation that utilizes image generators as an aesthetic prior. A reference image generated from the same prompt conditions the code model as input and provides visual signals during training. • We propose AesCode, which introduces decoupled cross-modal rewards driven by a design graph. It pairs deterministic verifiers for structural correctness with a sample-specific, graph-based VLM judge for aesthetic quality. • We release an infographic benchmark that evaluates correctness and visual quality separately, with human-aligned visual scores. References help every model we test, and AesCode matches leading proprietary models visually while following the prompt more closely. Related Work Visual Design and Code Generation. Posters, slides, and infographics can be generated as images or code. Image generators such as PosterMaker [ 10 ] and BizGen [ 30 ] compose appealing pages, but still misrender text and data on dense content [ 37 ] , and their raster outputs cannot be edited. Code is editable and verifiable. When written from text alone, as in LIDA [ 7 ] and PPTAgent [ 45 ] , it is composed without seeing the page and often looks plain. When written from an image, as in Design2Code [ 36 ] and ChartMimic [ 41 ] , it copies the input as ground truth. Closest to ours, DesignAsCode [ 26 ] and Editable Visual Design [ 43 ] let a coding agent consult a generated image, but only at inference time; the code model is never trained to use it. We instead train the code model to follow a prompt-generated image as an aesthetic prior for layout and style. Reward Design for Visual Generation. RL training requires a reward for the rendered page. In image-to-code, this reward is usually similarity to the input image, measured with visual metrics [ 33 , 3 ] or MLLM critics [ 42 , 21 ] . For a generated reference, however, this would penalize valid alternatives and reward copied errors. Without a target image, rule-based rewards are precise but limited to what a program can check, such as element overlap in AeSlides [ 28 ] , while holistic MLLM judges [ 46 , 2 ] give scores that shift with prompt phrasing. A more stable alternative breaks one judgment into many yes/no questions, first for text-to-image evaluation [ 4 ] and more recently as rubric rewards for RL [ 12 , 31 ] . These questions, however, are derived from text alone and cannot check the design a reference proposes. We therefore build a design graph from the prompt and the reference, verify code-level properties with rules, and turn the remaining visual properties into a Visual Graph Rubric (VGR) tied to graph elements. Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning. Critic-free methods such as GRPO [ 35 ] normalize rewards within a sampled group and, following DeepSeek-R1 [ 13 ] , have become a standard recipe for post-training LLMs and VLMs [ 25 ] . They assume a single reward, however: when several rewards are summed before normalization, a dense, near-saturated rule reward can drown out a sparse aesthetic one. MO-GRPO [ 16 ] reweights rewards by their variance, while GDPO [ 24 ] normalizes each reward separately. We adopt GDPO to balance our rule-based and VGR rewards. We first construct a target design graph that combines prompt-required content with non-authoritative reference cues ( Section 3.1 ). We then route its properties to deterministic and perceptual reward channels ( Section 3.2 ) and optimize them with SFT and GDPO [ 24 ] ( Section 3.3 ). items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.18851 (cs) [Submitted on 13 Oct 2026] Title: MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization Authors: Trieu Nguyen , Frazier N. Baker , Ruoxi Gao , Daniel Adu-Ampratwum , Xia Ning View a PDF of the paper titled MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization, by Trieu Nguyen and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Multi-objective molecular optimization is a critical process in drug discovery that aims to modify a given molecule to simultaneously improve multiple properties while maintaining a similar overall structure. This process often requires iterative modifications guided by computational or experimental feedback. Recent large language model (LLM)-based methods have begun to explore this iterative approach; however, these methods are not explicitly trained to leverage such feedback, while existing approaches primarily focus on single-turn molecular optimization. To address this gap, we introduce Multi-turn Feedback Guided (MFG) molecular optimization, a reinforcement learning framework that trains an LLM to progressively optimize molecules using feedback from previous turns. MFG introduces a feedback vector capturing both property improvements and source molecule similarity, alongside a feedback-aligned reward function that promotes progressive improvement across turns. We apply MFG over $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$, a state-of-the-art LLM model for multi-objective molecular optimization, evaluate $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ on ten multi-objective molecular optimization tasks. The results demonstrate that $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ achieves the highest average similarity-constrained success rate ($81.50%$), outperforming the base model $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$ ($70.81%$). Toward Physical Recursive Self-Improvement Authors: Hai Zhou , Fan Yang , Zeyi Chen , Lejun Zhang , Chenyang Fu , Jianping Li , Jiayi Zhu , Xianyang Liu , Yingxuan Yang , Lili Meng , Lu Wang , Xinyang Han , Jiankai Sun , Weirui Ye , Guanchu Wang , Wanhua Li , Ming Zhou , Boyi Li , Ming Jin , Kun Shao , Muhao Chen , Guang Chen , Lei Ma , Joey Tianyi Zhou , Costas Spanos , Xia Hu , Mac Schwager , Weinan Zhang , Qian Feng , Shangding Gu View a PDF of the paper titled Who Improves the Robot? Toward Physical Recursive Self-Improvement, by Hai Zhou and 29 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Robots are increasingly autonomous in task execution, yet their improvement remains largely human-driven. This study investigates Physical Recursive Self-Improvement (Physical RSI), in which physical experience guides lasting updates to both a robot's capabilities and its improvement procedure, making subsequent improvement more effective across tasks. Physical RSI faces challenges from noisy observations, continuous dynamics, costly trials, and irreversible consequences. We present an L0-L5 framework that differentiates capability-level from meta-level updates and within-task from across-task gains, reserving L5 for independently verified recursive gain. We study existing methods around harness adaptation and model training, alongside safety and control mechanisms that govern execution and successive updates. Our analysis reveals that, despite substantial progress in self-improvement, the surveyed literature does not yet demonstrate Physical RSI as defined by our framework. We identify research priorities in reliable feedback, causal attribution, safety preservation, and benchmarking, outlining a path toward robots that autonomously improve how they learn while ensuring safety. The GitHub repository for Physical RSI is available at this https URL . items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.18820 (cs) [Submitted on 13 Oct 2026 ( v1 ), last revised 14 Oct 2026 (this version, v2)] Title: Read the Room Before Your Model Generates Authors: Muyao Kong , Zhihao Lin View a PDF of the paper titled Read the Room Before Your Model Generates, by Muyao Kong and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generally rely on sampling temperature to regulate the amount of randomness in their outputs. Mainstream methods for selecting temperature typically involve fixed, heuristic global settings and context or token-level calibration, rather than a geometrically interpretable representation of the communicative scenario. In this work, we introduce a simple and interpretable temperature selection framework, the Scenario-Actor, which adapts decoding to the inferred situational characteristics. Scenario-Actor extracts scenario-relevant structures from Transformer hidden states and determines the temperature from scenario embedding, a structured geometric representation of the communicative setting. Empirical results show that on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Scenario-Actor achieves strong goal-completion performance in interactive social scenarios, significant gains on open-ended instruction following, and competitive performance on multi-turn conversation compared to multiple baselines.
