items.content: Read the Room Before Your Model Generates Muyao KongNew York University Email: muyao.kong@nyu.edu Zhihao Lin * Independent Researcher Email: zhihaolinsde@gmail.com Abstract Large language models (LLMs) generally rely on sampling temperature to regulate the amount of randomness in their outputs. Mainstream methods for selecting temperature typically involve fixed, heuristic global settings and context or token-level calibration, rather than a geometrically interpretable representation of the communicative scenario. In this work, we introduce a simple and interpretable temperature selection framework, the Scenario-Actor , which adapts decoding to the inferred situational characteristics. Scenario-Actor extracts scenario-relevant structures from Transformer hidden states and determines the temperature from scenario embedding, a structured geometric representation of the communicative setting. Empirical results show that on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Scenario-Actor achieves strong goal-completion performance in interactive social scenarios, significant gains on open-ended instruction following, and competitive performance on multi-turn conversation compared to multiple baselines. 1 1 footnotetext: Equal contribution. 2 2 footnotetext: Corresponding author. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) generate text by repeatedly sampling from a conditional next-token distribution. One of the simplest yet most consequential hyperparameters in language generation is the sampling temperature, which controls the sharpness of the next-token probability distribution and, in turn, the rigor and creativity of model output. Existing systems typically set it globally or adapt it according to predictive uncertainty, context, or learned decoding objectives, which implicitly treat decoding primarily as a property of the model’s predictive state ( Dhuliawala et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2020 ) . But socially situated language generation exposes a different source of variation: the interaction itself. A prompt conveys not only semantics but also implies a communicative setting. For example, the conversation could be either an academic discussion or a friendly chitchat, whose desired responses are either rigorous or open-ended, formal or casual. The optimal temperature is then circumstantial, varying across scenarios. Figure 1: AgentSense goal-outcome flip rate (top) and goal completion score (bottom) by changing temperature. In our controlled experiment, we decode 245 AgentSense ( Mou et al., 2025 ) social interactions with four fixed temperatures. We found that first, changing temperature substantially alters interaction quality, moving between mid-range temperatures flips 16 to 17% of individual goal outcomes; second, globally strongest temperature setting does not dominate across interactions. Such results show a major limitation of viewing temperature as a globally fixed hyperparameter, which motivates us to propose a way to control scenario-aware interaction and language generation. In this work, we propose Scenario-Actor , a framework for scenario-adaptive temperature selection. Scenario-Actor focuses on social interactions and open-ended instruction following, where the prompt provides enough evidence to infer a communicative scenario. We introduce a structured representation of the communicative setting extracted from context - the scenario embedding 1 1 1 In this work, we use the terms scenario vector and scenario embedding interchangeably. , whose span defines the scenario space, and use it to derive the sampling temperature. Specifically, our method maps a representation from the r r -th layer of the Transformer to an m m -dimensional scenario space, where each prompt is represented by a scenario embedding. An Actout \operatorname{Actout} function then maps the geometry of this vector to a prompt-level sampling. Prior work in social psychology provides us with a theoretical support by introducing DIAMONDS ( Rauthmann et al., 2014 ) , a working model of situation characteristics showing that human behavior varies with situation characteristics. We construct scenario axes from nine pre-defined scenario labels. At the end, five scenario axes are constructed, corresponding to five of the eight DIAMONDS - Duty, Intellect, Adversity, Negativity, and Sociality ( Rauthmann et al., 2014 ) . Evaluations across fixed and random temperature policies, nucleus sampling ( Holtzman et al., 2020 ) , and EDT ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) baselines indicate Scenario-Actor’s competitive performance on interactive social scenarios, open-ended instruction following, and multi-turn dialogue compared to most decoding strategies. 2 Background An autoregressive language model generates a response one token at a time. In each next-token generation, a trained neural network first produces a set of scores, which we call logits, from the prompt 𝒫 \mathcal{P} and the generated tokens over the vocabulary 𝒱 \mathcal{V} that represents all possible next tokens. A Softmax \operatorname{Softmax} function then transforms these logits to a distribution that gives how likely a token is to be the next. Let y t y_{t} and y < t y_{<t} be the t t -th token to be generated and already generated, and z t , v z_{t,v} be the t t -th logits of the token v v in the vocabulary. Concretely, we have Pr ⁡ ( y t = v ∣ P , y < t ) = exp ⁡ ( z t , v ) ∑ u ∈ 𝒱 exp ⁡ ( z t , u ) \Pr(y_{t}=v\mid P,y_{<t})=\frac{\exp(z_{t,v})}{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(z_{t,u})} Now, notice that if we divide each logit z t , v z_{t,v} with a positive scalar T T , the relative contribution of each numerator to the denominator will change with T T . When T > 1 T>1 , each exp ⁡ ( z t , v ) \exp(z_{t,v}) becomes less dominant over ∑ u ∈ 𝒱 exp ⁡ ( z t , u ) \sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(z_{t,u}) , making the probabilities more evenly distributed. When 0 < T < 1 0<T<1 , each exp ⁡ ( z t , v ) \exp(z_{t,v}) becomes more dominant. This scalar therefore controls the sharpness of the next-token distribution, which is commonly referred to as the temperature. Formally, for T > 0 T>0 , Pr ⁡ ( y t = v ∣ P , y < t ) = exp ⁡ ( z t , v T ) ∑ u ∈ 𝒱 exp ⁡ ( z t , u T ) \Pr(y_{t}=v\mid P,y_{<t})=\frac{\exp(\frac{z_{t,v}}{T})}{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(\frac{z_{t,u}}{T})} With all these, the last thing we need to do is to select a token through a process called sampling. Recent work center around language model’s temperature and sampling strategies, which we discuss in the following paragraphs. Fixed decoding hyperparameters. Early work and much of engineering practice predominantly relied on manually chosen global decoding strategies for task-specific models, such as beam search, top-k, and fixed sampling temperatures. Holtzman et al. (2020) showed that in open-ended text generation, likelihood-maximizing decoding methods often lead to bland, repetitive, and degenerate outputs, and proposed nucleus sampling (top- p p ) as a more effective alternative. Zhang et al. (2021) examined the trade-off between quality and diversity in different decoding strategies. Their findings indicate that all decoding methods perform similarly when diversity is a priority, but nucleus sampling ( Holtzman et al., 2020 ) consistently outperforms all other evaluated algorithms when quality is viewed as more important. Wiher et al. (2022) revealed that the effectiveness of decoding strategies is highly task-dependent. Later in LLM era, Shi et al. (2024) made a more systematic horizontal comparison among decoding methods and revealed that decoding method performance strongly depends on task, model size, alignment, and quantization. Figure 2: The Scenarize \operatorname{Scenarize} module. Token-level dynamic temperature. Fixed decoding hyperparameters are not always optimal at every decoding step. An early token-level architecture begins with Chang et al. (2023) , who proposed to relax the fixed-temperature assumption and adjust temperature dynamically according to its relevance to the source through KL-divergence. Zhu et al. (2024) then introduced AdapT sampling for code generation. Zhang et al. (2024) further put forth EDT, which adjusts temperature directly from token-level entropy to better balance quality and diversity. Context and example-level temperature. Another line of work concerns selecting sampling temperature from context. Wang et al. (2020) proposed contextual temperature, which learns a context-dependent temperature vector over the output vocabulary. Li et al. (2024) proposed DDS for open-domain dialogue system. DDS copes with two situations - chit-chat and factual QA - and maps context-dependent diversity score to a single decoding temperature. Dhuliawala et al. (2024) introduced adaptive decoding, which allows temperature to be predicted either once per example or dynamically at each decoding step. 3 The Scenario-Actor Most modern LLMs are built using the celebrated Transformer architecture. In our framework, we assume that our prompt context is represented by a Transformer model and take the r r -th layer hidden-state matrix as input. The Scenario-Actor has two fundamental parts: Scenarize \operatorname{Scenarize} and Actout \operatorname{Actout} . 2 2 2 The module names Scenarize and Actout reflect our view that a prompt induces a latent scenario, and the model acts out, or decodes, from that scenario accordingly. Scenarize \operatorname{Scenarize} takes the hidden-state matrix at the r r -th Transformer layer as its input and outputs the scenario embedding ; Actout \operatorname{Actout} takes a scenario embedding and maps it to a prompt-level sampling temperature T T . Figure 3: The Scenario-Actor - framework overview. In the remainder of this section, we discuss these two modules in depth. 3.1 Scenarize Before introducing our first module, let’s establish some basic mathematical setup. For a prompt 𝒫 = { p 1 , … , p l } \mathcal{P}=\{p_{1},\dots,p_{l}\} with l l tokens, let H 𝒫 ( r ) = [ h p 1 ( r ) , … , h p l ( r ) ] T ∈ ℝ l × d H_{\mathcal{P}}^{(r)}=[h_{p_{1}}^{(r)},\dots,h_{p_{l}}^{(r)}]^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{l\times d} denote the hidden-state matrix at the r r -th Transformer layer, and s 𝒫 ∈ 𝒮 ⊆ ℝ m s_{\mathcal{P}}\in\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} denote the learned m m -dimensional scenario embedding of prompt 𝒫 \mathcal{P} . The set S ≔ { s 𝒫 | s 𝒫 = Scenarize ⁡ ( H 𝒫 ( r ) ) ∈ ℝ m } S\coloneqq\left\{s_{\mathcal{P}}\;\middle|\;s_{\mathcal{P}}=\operatorname{Scenarize}(H_{\mathcal{P}}^{(r)})\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\right\} be the set of all learned scenario embeddings. We define the scenario space as 𝒮 ≔ span ⁡ ( S ) ⊆ ℝ m . \mathcal{S}\coloneqq\operatorname{span}(S)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}. Given that the language model interaction is text-only, the underlying prompt scenario is often under-determined with shorter linguistic sequences. As more tokens are observed, the scenario is generally expected to be more identifiable since longer prompts typically provide additional disambiguating context. As such, we model Scenarize ⁡ ( H 𝒫 ( r ) ) \operatorname{Scenarize}(H^{(r)}_{\mathcal{P}}) as a recurrent neural network (RNN) that updates the inferred scenario token by token. The final state at p l p_{l} therefore represents the most informed scenario embedding which we will consider. Overall, we compute scenario embedding as s t \displaystyle s_{t} = Scenarize ⁡ ( h p t ( r ) ) \displaystyle=\operatorname{Scenarize}(h_{p_{t}}^{(r)}) (1) = ϕ ⁡ ( U stm ​ s t − 1 + W smm ​ h p t ( r ) + b ) \displaystyle=\phi(U_{\text{stm}}s_{t-1}+W_{\text{smm}}h_{p_{t}}^{(r)}+b) Here, ϕ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \phi(\cdot) is the activation function; U stm ∈ ℝ m × m U_{\text{stm}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} is the scenario transition matrix (STM); W smm ∈ ℝ m × d W_{\text{smm}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} is the scenario mapping matrix (SMM); and b ∈ ℝ m b\in\mathbb{R}^{m} is the bias term. Each scenario vector is computed as the learned affine combination of the previous token estimate and the current inference from context h p t ( r ) ∈ H 𝒫 ( r ) h_{p_{t}}^{(r)}\in H_{\mathcal{P}}^{(r)} , as depicted in Figure 2 . Both STM and SMM are expected to be trained on prompt triplets ( 𝒫 , 𝒫 + , 𝒫 − ) (\mathcal{P},\mathcal{P}^{+},\mathcal{P}^{-}) , where 𝒫 \mathcal{P} denotes the prompt with base scenario, 𝒫 + \mathcal{P}^{+} the prompt with similar scenario, and 𝒫 − \mathcal{P}^{-} the prompt with opposite scenario. Given such a triplet, we define the loss function as ℒ = max ⁡ ( 0 , d ⁡ ( s 𝒫 , s 𝒫 + ) − d ⁡ ( s 𝒫 , s 𝒫 − ) + β ) \mathcal{L}=\max(0,d(s_{\mathcal{P}},s_{\mathcal{P}^{+}})-d(s_{\mathcal{P}},s_{\mathcal{P}^{-}})+\beta) (2) which compares the distance from the base prompt scenario vector to the similar and opposite scenario vector with a margin β \beta . In this work, we employ the squared Euclidean distance d ⁡ ( s 𝒫 , s 𝒫 + ) = ∥ s 𝒫 − s 𝒫 + ∥ 2 d(s_{\mathcal{P}},s_{\mathcal{P}^{+}})=\lVert s_{\mathcal{P}}-s_{\mathcal{P}^{+}}\rVert^{2} and d ⁡ ( s 𝒫 , s 𝒫 − ) = ∥ s 𝒫 − s 𝒫 − ∥ 2 d(s_{\mathcal{P}},s_{\mathcal{P}^{-}})=\lVert s_{\mathcal{P}}-s_{\mathcal{P}^{-}}\rVert^{2} . 3.2 Actout Actout \operatorname{Actout} maps a scenario embedding to a temperature. Drawing on SemAxis ( An et al., 2018 ) , we define scenario axes from two non-zero opposite scenario vectors s + s^{+} and s − s^{-} . Each scenario axis u i u_{i} can be defined as u i = s i + − s i − ∈ ℝ m u_{i}=s_{i}^{+}-s_{i}^{-}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} . We name the scenario vectors on all scenario axes as subscenario vectors , each representing an elementary component of a more complex scenario. For all scenario axes, two typical temperatures τ i + \tau_{i}^{+} and τ i − \tau_{i}^{-} on both the positive and negative directions are applied. In general, u 1 , … , u k u_{1},\dots,u_{k} have one-to-one correspondence with ( τ 1 + , τ 1 − ) , … , ( τ k + , τ k − ) ∈ ℝ ≥ 0 × ℝ ≥ 0 (\tau_{1}^{+},\tau_{1}^{-}),\dots,(\tau_{k}^{+},\tau_{k}^{-})\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\times\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} . Let ρ i = s ^ 𝒫 ⊤ ​ u ^ i \rho_{i}=\hat{s}_{\mathcal{P}}^{\top}\hat{u}_{i} be the signed cosine similarity between the normalized scenario embedding and the axis. For ∑ i = 1 k | ρ i | > 0 \sum_{i=1}^{k}|\rho_{i}|>0 , the prompt-level temperature T T is then defined as T = ∑ i = 1 k | ρ i | ( 1 + ρ i 2 ​ τ i + + 1 − ρ i 2 ​ τ i − ) ∑ i = 1 k | ρ i | T=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k}|\rho_{i}|\left(\frac{1+\rho_{i}}{2}\tau_{i}^{+}+\frac{1-\rho_{i}}{2}\tau_{i}^{-}\right)}{\sum_{i=1}^{k}|\rho_{i}|} (3) Temperature is defined as a normalized weighted average over k k scenario axes. For each axis u ^ i \hat{u}_{i} , the cosine similarity ρ i \rho_{i} specifies where the scenario embedding lies along that axis. Endpoint temperatures τ i + \tau_{i}^{+} and τ i − \tau_{i}^{-} are linearly interpolated based on ρ i \rho_{i} , so that the estimate moves towards τ i + \tau_{i}^{+} if ρ i \rho_{i} is positive and τ i − \tau_{i}^{-} if negative. The denominator normalizes the weighted sum, eventually yielding a temperature inferred from the prompt’s position in scenario space. 4 Experiment We evaluate our proposed Scenario-Actor framework on benchmarks covering interactive social scenarios, open-ended instruction following and multi-turn question answering to test its performance on context-rich and socially-situated interactions. We also use GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) as a task-only stress test to study the boundary of scenario-based decoding. 4.1 Experimental Setup 4.1.1 Backbone model Despite the outstanding performance of mainstream LLMs such as ChatGPT and Gemini, we do not have access to the hidden states with API calls. Therefore, we use the open-weight Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) as our backbone model. The model is used for both hidden-state extraction and generation. 4.1.2 Data We collect 37,357 conversational prompts from human-human and human-LLM interaction corpora, including WildChat ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) and DailyDialog ( Li et al., 2017 ) , together with targeted supplementary datasets for under-represented scenario types. Each prompt is annotated by GPT-4o ( OpenAI, 2024 ) with one of nine scenario labels. A confidence-based filtering is applied to construct a high-confidence supervision set, resulting in 34,427 training prompts for triplet construction and 2,930 validation prompts. 4.1.3 Baselines We compare Scenario-Actor against fixed-temperature decoding at T ∈ { 0.5 , 0.7 , 1.0 , 1.5 } T\in\{0.5,0.7,1.0,1.5\} , greedy decoding, random temperature selection, nucleus sampling ( Holtzman et al., 2020 ) with p = 0.95 p=0.95 and T = 1.0 T=1.0 , and entropy-driven temperature decoding (EDT) ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) . EDT is included as a training-free and directly reproducible adaptive baseline. DDS and LPO ( Li et al., 2024 ; Dhuliawala et al., 2024 ) both, in contrast, require training additional components. LPO trains its decoder module via preference optimization over sampled outputs, and DDS trains a diversity regressor designed for a two-way chit-chat vs. QA distinction, with, to our knowledge, no public implementation. Reproducing either method involves substantial heuristic design choices of our own, making the comparison hard to attribute in either direction. 4.1.4 Implementation details Hidden states Llama-3.1-8B has 32 Transformer layers. For all experiments, we use the hidden states at the 16th Transformer layer. We found that scenario geometry collapses with deeper Transformer layer, which we discuss in Section 4.4 . Scenarize Scenarize \operatorname{Scenarize} maps the above hidden states into a 32-dimensional scenario embedding. The implementation follows Equation 1 , where r = 16 r=16 is the Transformer layer, ϕ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) = tanh ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \phi(\cdot)=\operatorname{tanh}(\cdot) is the activation function. Scenarize \operatorname{Scenarize} is trained according to Equation 2 with squared Euclidean triplet loss with margin β = 0.3 \beta=0.3 . AdamW with learning rate 3.0e-4, weight decay 1.0e-4, gradient clipping at 1.0, and early stopping based on validation recall@1 is used as optimizer. items.raw_text: Read the Room Before Your Model Generates Muyao KongNew York University Email: muyao.kong@nyu.edu Zhihao Lin * Independent Researcher Email: zhihaolinsde@gmail.com Abstract Large language models (LLMs) generally rely on sampling temperature to regulate the amount of randomness in their outputs. Mainstream methods for selecting temperature typically involve fixed, heuristic global settings and context or token-level calibration, rather than a geometrically interpretable representation of the communicative scenario. In this work, we introduce a simple and interpretable temperature selection framework, the Scenario-Actor , which adapts decoding to the inferred situational characteristics. Scenario-Actor extracts scenario-relevant structures from Transformer hidden states and determines the temperature from scenario embedding, a structured geometric representation of the communicative setting. Empirical results show that on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Scenario-Actor achieves strong goal-completion performance in interactive social scenarios, significant gains on open-ended instruction following, and competitive performance on multi-turn conversation compared to multiple baselines. 1 1 footnotetext: Equal contribution. 2 2 footnotetext: Corresponding author. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) generate text by repeatedly sampling from a conditional next-token distribution. One of the simplest yet most consequential hyperparameters in language generation is the sampling temperature, which controls the sharpness of the next-token probability distribution and, in turn, the rigor and creativity of model output. Existing systems typically set it globally or adapt it according to predictive uncertainty, context, or learned decoding objectives, which implicitly treat decoding primarily as a property of the model’s predictive state ( Dhuliawala et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2020 ) . But socially situated language generation exposes a different source of variation: the interaction itself. A prompt conveys not only semantics but also implies a communicative setting. For example, the conversation could be either an academic discussion or a friendly chitchat, whose desired responses are either rigorous or open-ended, formal or casual. The optimal temperature is then circumstantial, varying across scenarios. Figure 1: AgentSense goal-outcome flip rate (top) and goal completion score (bottom) by changing temperature. In our controlled experiment, we decode 245 AgentSense ( Mou et al., 2025 ) social interactions with four fixed temperatures. We found that first, changing temperature substantially alters interaction quality, moving between mid-range temperatures flips 16 to 17% of individual goal outcomes; second, globally strongest temperature setting does not dominate across interactions. Such results show a major limitation of viewing temperature as a globally fixed hyperparameter, which motivates us to propose a way to control scenario-aware interaction and language generation. In this work, we propose Scenario-Actor , a framework for scenario-adaptive temperature selection. Scenario-Actor focuses on social interactions and open-ended instruction following, where the prompt provides enough evidence to infer a communicative scenario. We introduce a structured representation of the communicative setting extracted from context - the scenario embedding 1 1 1 In this work, we use the terms scenario vector and scenario embedding interchangeably. , whose span defines the scenario space, and use it to derive the sampling temperature. Specifically, our method maps a representation from the r r -th layer of the Transformer to an m m -dimensional scenario space, where each prompt is represented by a scenario embedding. An Actout \operatorname{Actout} function then maps the geometry of this vector to a prompt-level sampling. Prior work in social psychology provides us with a theoretical support by introducing DIAMONDS ( Rauthmann et al., 2014 ) , a working model of situation characteristics showing that human behavior varies with situation characteristics. We construct scenario axes from nine pre-defined scenario labels. At the end, five scenario axes are constructed, corresponding to five of the eight DIAMONDS - Duty, Intellect, Adversity, Negativity, and Sociality ( Rauthmann et al., 2014 ) . Evaluations across fixed and random temperature policies, nucleus sampling ( Holtzman et al., 2020 ) , and EDT ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) baselines indicate Scenario-Actor’s competitive performance on interactive social scenarios, open-ended instruction following, and multi-turn dialogue compared to most decoding strategies. 2 Background An autoregressive language model generates a response one token at a time. In each next-token generation, a trained neural network first produces a set of scores, which we call logits, from the prompt 𝒫 \mathcal{P} and the generated tokens over the vocabulary 𝒱 \mathcal{V} that represents all possible next tokens. A Softmax \operatorname{Softmax} function then transforms these logits to a distribution that gives how likely a token is to be the next. Let y t y_{t} and y < t y_{<t} be the t t -th token to be generated and already generated, and z t , v z_{t,v} be the t t -th logits of the token v v in the vocabulary. Concretely, we have Pr ⁡ ( y t = v ∣ P , y < t ) = exp ⁡ ( z t , v ) ∑ u ∈ 𝒱 exp ⁡ ( z t , u ) \Pr(y_{t}=v\mid P,y_{<t})=\frac{\exp(z_{t,v})}{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(z_{t,u})} Now, notice that if we divide each logit z t , v z_{t,v} with a positive scalar T T , the relative contribution of each numerator to the denominator will change with T T . When T > 1 T>1 , each exp ⁡ ( z t , v ) \exp(z_{t,v}) becomes less dominant over ∑ u ∈ 𝒱 exp ⁡ ( z t , u ) \sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(z_{t,u}) , making the probabilities more evenly distributed. When 0 < T < 1 0<T<1 , each exp ⁡ ( z t , v ) \exp(z_{t,v}) becomes more dominant. This scalar therefore controls the sharpness of the next-token distribution, which is commonly referred to as the temperature. Formally, for T > 0 T>0 , Pr ⁡ ( y t = v ∣ P , y < t ) = exp ⁡ ( z t , v T ) ∑ u ∈ 𝒱 exp ⁡ ( z t , u T ) \Pr(y_{t}=v\mid P,y_{<t})=\frac{\exp(\frac{z_{t,v}}{T})}{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(\frac{z_{t,u}}{T})} With all these, the last thing we need to do is to select a token through a process called sampling. Recent work center around language model’s temperature and sampling strategies, which we discuss in the following paragraphs. Fixed decoding hyperparameters. Early work and much of engineering practice predominantly relied on manually chosen global decoding strategies for task-specific models, such as beam search, top-k, and fixed sampling temperatures. Holtzman et al. (2020) showed that in open-ended text generation, likelihood-maximizing decoding methods often lead to bland, repetitive, and degenerate outputs, and proposed nucleus sampling (top- p p ) as a more effective alternative. Zhang et al. (2021) examined the trade-off between quality and diversity in different decoding strategies. Their findings indicate that all decoding methods perform similarly when diversity is a priority, but nucleus sampling ( Holtzman et al., 2020 ) consistently outperforms all other evaluated algorithms when quality is viewed as more important. Wiher et al. (2022) revealed that the effectiveness of decoding strategies is highly task-dependent. Later in LLM era, Shi et al. (2024) made a more systematic horizontal comparison among decoding methods and revealed that decoding method performance strongly depends on task, model size, alignment, and quantization. Figure 2: The Scenarize \operatorname{Scenarize} module. Token-level dynamic temperature. Fixed decoding hyperparameters are not always optimal at every decoding step. An early token-level architecture begins with Chang et al. (2023) , who proposed to relax the fixed-temperature assumption and adjust temperature dynamically according to its relevance to the source through KL-divergence. Zhu et al. (2024) then introduced AdapT sampling for code generation. Zhang et al. (2024) further put forth EDT, which adjusts temperature directly from token-level entropy to better balance quality and diversity. Context and example-level temperature. Another line of work concerns selecting sampling temperature from context. Wang et al. (2020) proposed contextual temperature, which learns a context-dependent temperature vector over the output vocabulary. Li et al. (2024) proposed DDS for open-domain dialogue system. DDS copes with two situations - chit-chat and factual QA - and maps context-dependent diversity score to a single decoding temperature. Dhuliawala et al. (2024) introduced adaptive decoding, which allows temperature to be predicted either once per example or dynamically at each decoding step. 3 The Scenario-Actor Most modern LLMs are built using the celebrated Transformer architecture. In our framework, we assume that our prompt context is represented by a Transformer model and take the r r -th layer hidden-state matrix as input. The Scenario-Actor has two fundamental parts: Scenarize \operatorname{Scenarize} and Actout \operatorname{Actout} . 2 2 2 The module names Scenarize and Actout reflect our view that a prompt induces a latent scenario, and the model acts out, or decodes, from that scenario accordingly. Scenarize \operatorname{Scenarize} takes the hidden-state matrix at the r r -th Transformer layer as its input and outputs the scenario embedding ; Actout \operatorname{Actout} takes a scenario embedding and maps it to a prompt-level sampling temperature T T . items.content: At a glance End-to-end forecasting: A machine learning pipeline uses forecast-time solar-wind information to generate location-specific risk estimates for 66,935 substations in the continental United States. Physics and place: The system combines Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) forecasts with local latitude, geology, and ground conductivity. Advance warning: The pipeline detected nearly 80% of major space-weather events during the evaluation period and can warn grid operators 30 to 60 minutes before a specific risk appears. Forecasting a threat to critical infrastructure During the May 2024 geomagnetic storm, utilities across North America prepared for possible impacts as auroras extended far beyond their usual range. The storm would degrade GPS accuracy and satellite operations, impacting farm operations in North America and Europe. Modern society depends on reliable electric power, yet extreme space-weather events can induce currents in transmission networks that damage equipment and increase operational risk. The challenge is not only knowing that a storm is approaching, but estimating when and where its effects could be most severe with enough warning for grid operators to respond. During my summer internship at Microsoft Research, I developed a machine learning system that forecasts space-weather risk across 66,935 substations in the continental United States. The system measures how the sun’s activity can affect the earth’s magnetic field and, ultimately, the power grid. It combines solar-wind observations, forecasts of the Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) indices, physics-informed constraints, local geological conductivity, and grid-infrastructure data to produce location-specific risk estimates 30-60 minutes ahead of potential impact. Building an end-to-end prediction pipeline Space-weather prediction is difficult because it spans several coupled systems. The solar wind changes rapidly, its interaction with Earth’s magnetosphere is irregular, and the resulting ground effects depend on local conditions. Regions with resistive bedrock can experience stronger geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) than regions with more conductive geology. Transmission-line orientation, latitude, and other power-system characteristics further influence the exposure of individual assets. Spotlight: Microsoft research newsletter Microsoft Research Newsletter Stay connected to the research community at Microsoft. Subscribe today Opens in a new tab The pipeline addresses this complexity in three stages, shown in Figure 1. First, solar-wind measurements from the L1 Lagrange point are used to generate forecasts of the AE and Dst indices, while geological conductivity and location features are assembled for each substation. Second, a gradient-boosting model combines these forecasted and location-specific inputs to estimate dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC risk. Finally, the resulting predictions are converted into location-specific risk estimates and aggregated into a continental risk assessment. A system of 50 AI agents helped explore features, validation strategies, and model configurations across the pipeline. Only public data sources were used, included NASA OMNI and NASA-aggregated Kyoto World Data Center data, INTERMAGNET and U.S. Geological Survey magnetometer observations, and GridSFM-derived grid data. Figure 1. End-to-end forecasting pipeline from L1 solar-wind measurements to location-specific risk estimates across 66,935 U.S. substations. Evaluating geomagnetic forecasts and infrastructure risk The AE predictor was designed to forecast rare, high-intensity geomagnetic activity that drives infrastructure risk. In the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the model produced forecasts spanning nearly the full observed range of AE activity and outperformed several empirical solar-wind-based approaches. The Dst predictor provided an additional signal describing large-scale geomagnetic storm strength. During the most geomagnetically active periods of the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the machine-learning model outperformed the Burton equation on 62.2% of individual hours. The model also produced a substantially wider prediction range than Burton-style approaches and improved severe-event detection in the end-to-end forecasting system by 1.2 percentage points when combined with AE forecasts. Predictor Result Baseline comparison Impact AE 410.2 nT RMSE Lower RMSE than empirical and solar-wind-only baselines Captures extreme-event activity used by the GIC forecasting system Dst 7.2 nT RMSE Outperformed Burton on 62.2% of peak-activity hours and provided wider prediction range +1.2pp severe storm detection when integrated into final GIC system The GIC risk stage was evaluated differently. There is no equivalent widely deployed operational system that provides a direct industry benchmark for this calculation, so the machine learning model was compared with simple linear regression. As Figure 2 shows, the system achieved detection rates of 76.5% for major events (≥10 nT/min), 81.2% for severe events (≥20 nT/min), and 64.1% for extreme events (≥50 nT/min). False-alarm rates increased with storm severity, reflecting the trade-off between missed events and cautious alerts. Performance varied by latitude, with the highest detection rates at northern stations where geomagnetic activity is strongest. Figure 2. Detection rates across storm-severity thresholds for regionally different substations, with a comparison between the average POD for each severity tier. Translating predictions into continental risk assessments The final stage translates predicted geomagnetic activity into location-specific estimates of dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC exposure. Rather than issuing a single alert for the continental United States, the system combines storm conditions with each substation’s latitude and geological factor. This produces continuous risk estimates that can distinguish lower-risk locations from areas where resistive geology can amplify ground-level effects. Figure 3 illustrates the output for a representative major-storm scenario. The map is a demonstration of the model’s continental-scale output, not a record of a live operational event. It shows how a grid operator or planner could move from a broad space-weather warning toward a more targeted view of which locations may warrant closer analysis. The current pipeline produced estimates for all 66,935 substations in approximately 333 milliseconds during measured inference, allowing many scenarios to be evaluated quickly. Figure 3. Demonstration of a continental GIC risk assessment under a representative major-storm scenario. Colors indicate modeled risk levels across 66,935 substations. Implications and looking forward This work demonstrates how physics-grounded machine learning could support more specific and timely assessment of space-weather exposure. Earlier, location-specific information could help utilities prioritize engineering review and consider targeted protective actions, such as adjusting reactive-power reserves or temporarily reconfiguring parts of the network. Further validation with utilities and operational data would be needed before the system could be used in grid operations. The project also connects with broader Microsoft Research work on AI for power systems. The open grid-data pipeline provided realistic U.S. transmission models, while GridSFM applies deep learning to AC optimal power flow for fast scenario analysis. Together, these efforts point toward richer planning and resilience workflows that combine hazard forecasts, grid topology, and power-flow analysis. Extend forecast horizons: Explore temporal-transformer approaches that capture longer-range patterns in solar-wind data and move beyond the current 30-60-minute window. Scale internationally: Adapt the system to additional regions while accounting for different geological conditions and grid topologies. Integrate with grid operations: Evaluate how forecasts could support existing decision-making and engineering-review workflows before considering higher levels of automation. Provide transformer-level risk: Add asset-specific characteristics to move from substation-level estimates toward more granular assessments of critical equipment. Related Microsoft Research work Video playback requires cookie consent GridSFM: A new, small foundation model for the electric grid Building realistic electric transmission grid dataset at scale: a pipeline from open dataset Acknowledgements Special thanks to my mentors Weiwei Yang and Spencer Fowers for their guidance throughout this project, and to Amber Hoak , Weishung Liu , and Andrea Britto for their editorial and technical feedback. Weekly, monthly and annual rates are averages of business days unless otherwise noted. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: October 14, 2026 Back to Top
